meta.intent: Identify, consolidate and assemble the playbook material for the three capabilities the Data Asset Management (DAM) Policy rests on (data governance, data cataloguing and data quality) and publish it as one interactive portal on GitHub Pages, so that a lead policy coordinator, a data owner or a data steward has one place to start, can see what the policy requires, and can follow a method for each capability that joins up with the other two.

requirements.text: Identify the data assets in scope: classified OFFICIAL (including handling markings such as 'personal'), meeting the critical data asset criteria, and inside your own data ownership accountabilities.
Identify and manage metadata about in-scope assets within your data catalogues.
Report in-scope assets to GDS. Departments provide metadata on their assets and coordinate and assure the returns of their ALBs.
Maintain metadata and review it every year.
Every identified asset has a named data owner, accountable for decisions about the data.
Every identified asset has a data quality action plan (DQAP) or an equivalent mechanism for managing its quality.
Where you already manage the quality of critical data, review those processes to confirm they cover every step of the DQAP implementation guide.
The chief data officer of each in-scope organisation implements the policy; the Chief Data Officer Council oversees implementation; the minister writes to ministers each year on progress.

Choose an ownership option (keep the IAO model, adopt the data ownership model, or a hybrid) and still meet the mandatory IAO actions, with governance covering accountability, reporting lines, assurance and data quality.
When a data owner leaves, tell the coordinating team, have a successor ready and give the successor's details so the metadata can be updated.

Each critical data asset supports at least one of the seven purposes: public service delivery; legislative, legal or contractual requirement; defence, national security and resilience; policy development and evaluation; official statistics; public interest; fraud and error.
If you designate a particular distribution of a data set, designate its source data set as well.
Record the metadata properties set out in the metadata guidance, in plain English, with ISO 8601 dates and 'unknown' or 'not applicable' rather than blanks.

The chief data officer, or the most senior data official, leads identification and appoints a coordinating team or person, drawing in owners, IAOs, stewards, service owners, analysts and policy makers.

Prioritise quality issues with the issues framework: importance of purpose times impact sets the target range; the band below target sets priority. Its resolution timescales (Critical immediately; High, Medium and Low within 1, 3 and 6 measurements) are given as an example.

The policy's introduction promises minimum requirements for interoperability, but the policy body does not state them. Treat the metadata guidance and the MEM as the current interoperability baseline and watch for guidance (open item OR-05).

roles.name: Chief data officer
roles.text: Implements the policy in the organisation and leads the identification exercise; sponsors governance.

roles.name: Lead policy coordinator
roles.text: Coordinates identification, collates and assures the return (including ALBs), and is the link to the Working Group.

roles.name: Data governance board
roles.text: Sets policy direction, resolves escalations and sees every asset's status. Chaired by the CDO, SIRO or equivalent.

roles.name: Data owner
roles.text: Senior leader accountable for the meaning, content, quality and management of the asset; approves changes and signs off targets and risks.

roles.name: Information asset owner
roles.text: Accountable to the SIRO for protecting the whole information asset; may hold data owner duties under the IAO or hybrid option.

roles.name: Data steward
roles.text: Runs the asset day to day: policies and standards, access, quality processes and documentation such as the business glossary in the catalogue.

roles.name: Data custodian
roles.text: Technical expert for the system holding the data: storage, access controls, auditable change and disposal.

roles.name: Catalogue manager
roles.text: Runs the organisation's catalogue, its metadata standard and its harvest feed.

roles.name: Data quality lead or analyst
roles.text: Methods, profiling, tooling and reporting for data quality.

roles.name: Data protection officer
roles.text: Independent advice on lawful basis, DPIAs and data subject rights.

roles.name: Data users
roles.text: Teams, services and other organisations that rely on the data; say what they need and report problems.

roles.name: People the data describes
roles.text: Citizens, communities and their representatives; help spot exclusion and test whether quality information is understandable.

roles.name: Senior responsible owner
roles.text: Accountable for a programme or project meeting its objectives. Makes sure data assets the change creates, alters or retires have owners, budgets and assurance, and signs off handover to business as usual.

roles.name: Programme or project manager
roles.text: Plans and runs the change. Builds DAM activities into the plan, the risk register and gate criteria, and makes sure data owners are consulted at each stage.

roles.name: Service or product owner
roles.text: Owns the service the change delivers. Decides what data the service collects and exposes, and shows DAM evidence at service assessments.

roles.name: Design authority or solution architect
roles.text: Approves data models, platforms and integrations. Checks new designs use open standards, documented schemas and an exit route, so they do not become future legacy.

roles.name: Data migration lead
roles.text: Plans and runs data migration. Profiles quality before moving data, reconciles after, and keeps catalogue entries and ownership in step.

roles.name: Commercial lead
roles.text: Runs procurement and manages contracts. Writes data ownership, metadata delivery, quality reporting and exit into contracts.

roles.name: Programme office and assurance
roles.text: Tracks delivery and organises assurance reviews. Checks DAM checkpoints are met at each gate and reports gaps to the senior responsible owner.

in_brief: Every critical data asset needs a named data owner. Governance is how you appoint them and keep them active.
Run five recipes in order the first time, then as a yearly loop.
Record decisions, issues and exceptions as you go, so your evidence for GDS builds itself.
before_you_start: Agreement from your chief data officer to lead adoption
A list of the data policies you already have, however informal
Your organisation's choice, or shortlist, of ownership option
you_get: An evidence pack for the GDS return
capabilities.name: Data governance
capabilities.question: Who decides, by what authority, and how do we know it is working?
capabilities.purpose: Put the authority, roles and routines in place so that every critical data asset has a named, active owner, decisions are made and recorded, and the organisation can evidence its DAM Policy adoption.
capabilities.why: The policy requires a named data owner for every asset (DAM-R05), an ownership option that still meets the mandatory IAO actions (DAM-R09), and CDO-led implementation under CDO Council oversight (DAM-R08).
capabilities.method_intro: Five repeatable recipes: Mandate, Frame, Assign, Operate and Assure. Run them in order the first time, then as a loop, with Assure feeding lessons back into Mandate. The sequence comes from the cross-government Data Governance Playbook (practitioner draft); the requirements it meets come from GDS guidance.

stages.name: Mandate
stages.goal: Establish the authority everything else operates under.
stages.trigger: A new governance need, the start of DAM Policy adoption, or the annual refresh.
steps: Confirm the sponsor (the CDO, SIRO or equivalent) who will chair or co-sign the charter.
Draft a one-page charter covering purpose, scope, authority and review cadence.
State which data, systems and decisions are in scope, and any exclusions. Start narrow, with critical data assets.
Route the charter for approval and record the decision and its date.
Publish it to every stakeholder found during scoping.
checklist: Sponsor confirmed in writing
Scope covers every critical data asset the organisation owns
Sign-off obtained and dated
Review date set, at least annual
stages.tip: A charter that tries to cover everything is approved slowly or not at all. Widen scope at the annual refresh once the model works.

stages.name: Frame
stages.goal: Assemble a proportionate rulebook to make decisions against.
stages.trigger: The charter is approved and policy gaps are known.
steps: List every data policy and standard already in force, however informal.
Compare it with the core areas - governance, classification and handling, quality, retention and disposal, access and sharing, metadata, master and reference data, and ethics including AI use.
Draft or adopt what is missing, in proportion to the risk. Reuse cross-government guidance before writing your own.
Give every policy a named owner (a role) and a review date.
Register each policy and make it findable, ideally in the data catalogue.
outputs: Policy owner list with review dates
checklist: Gap assessment against the core areas done
Every policy has an owner role and a review date
The register is published and findable
stages.tip: Adopting a cross-government template keeps you consistent with other departments and makes shared assurance easier.

stages.name: Assign
stages.goal: Put a named, accountable owner and an active steward against every critical data asset.
stages.trigger: Policies are adopted and critical assets lack named owners.
steps: Choose your ownership option - IAO model, data ownership model or hybrid - and record the decision.
For each critical data asset, propose an owner of matching seniority (SCS for large or complex assets; Grade 6 or 7 for smaller ones), a steward and a custodian.
Agree decision rights using the RACI below and any delegated thresholds.
Brief role holders and record training (Data Owner and Steward training).
Record owner, steward, custodian, effective date and a named successor in the ownership register and the catalogue record.
outputs: RACI per asset or asset class
checklist: Every critical data asset has a named owner
Every role has a named deputy or successor
The catalogue record shows the owner role and a contact point that is a team or form, never a personal inbox
Mandatory IAO actions still covered whichever option you chose
stages.tip: A single point of failure in accountability is the most common finding when this step is audited. Name a backup for every owner and steward.

stages.name: Operate
stages.goal: Make governance visible day to day.
stages.trigger: Owners are in place and governance moves into business as usual.
steps: Set the board's cadence (monthly, at least quarterly) and publish the calendar.
Keep a decision log - what, who, why, when and the review trigger.
Keep an issue and risk log, with quality issues coming in from the DQAP.
Log every deviation from policy as an exception with an owner and an expiry date.
Escalate anything unresolved up the ladder.
checklist: Decision log active and current
Every exception has an expiry date
Escalations tracked to resolution
Minutes published within five working days
stages.tip: An empty decision log after three months is a warning, not efficiency. Decisions are being made off the record.

stages.name: Assure
stages.goal: Prove it works and feed the lessons back into the mandate.
stages.trigger: A reporting cycle, the annual return or an audit is due.
steps: Re-run the data maturity self-assessment.
Compile measures from the live registers - owner coverage, review currency, DQAP coverage, exceptions.
Map evidence to the GDS annual return as you go, not at the deadline.
Have someone outside the board check the evidence before submission.
Submit, then log lessons back into Mandate.
outputs: Evidence pack mapped to the GDS return
checklist: Evidence collected continuously during Operate
Independent check done before submission
Return submitted on time
Lessons logged to Mandate
stages.tip: Keep an evidence folder updated every time a decision is logged, so the return is collation, not reconstruction.

in_brief: Find the data other organisations depend on, and decide which of it is critical.
Describe each critical data asset well enough for someone outside your team to find and judge it.
Keep the descriptions in a catalogue, report them to GDS, and review them every year.
before_you_start: A named coordinating team, led by your chief data officer
Access to your data catalogue, information asset register and register of data sharing agreements
Ownership confirmed, or under way, through the governance Assign recipe
capabilities.name: Data cataloguing
capabilities.question: What critical data do we hold, is it described well enough to find and reuse, and have we told GDS?
capabilities.purpose: Find the critical data assets, describe each one to the cross-government metadata standard, keep the descriptions in a catalogue that others can harvest, and report them to GDS every year.
capabilities.why: Identifying, cataloguing, reporting and annually reviewing metadata are all 'must' requirements (DAM-R01 to DAM-R04).
capabilities.method_intro: Eight stages from mobilising the team to the annual review. The sequence is this playbook's synthesis of the policy, the identification guidance and the metadata guidance; each step points to the requirement it meets. The internal Data Cataloguing Playbook (v2.6) is the fuller source and is not yet public (open item OR-01).

stages.name: Mobilise
stages.goal: Have a named lead and a coordinating team before identification starts.
stages.trigger: Policy adoption begins, or a new reporting cycle opens.
steps: The CDO (or most senior data official) leads and appoints a coordinating team or person.
Nominate the lead policy coordinator for the Working Group.
Agree how the department will coordinate and assure its ALBs' returns.
Bring in data owners, IAOs, stewards, service owners, analysts and policy makers.
checklist: Coordinator nominated to the Working Group
Every ALB has a named contact role

stages.name: Discover candidates
stages.goal: Build a long list of data other organisations depend on.
steps: Start from what you already have - data catalogues, information asset registers and registers of data sharing agreements.
Find data you provide to, or acquire from, other organisations for an essential process or purpose.
Prioritise assets supporting government missions and your services (including Top 75 services).
Include high-reuse-value assets not yet shared.
outputs: Candidate list with source of each entry
checklist: All three starting registers searched
Both directions covered - data provided and data acquired

stages.name: Test and designate
stages.goal: Decide which candidates are critical data assets, and draw each asset's boundary.
steps: Apply the policy's scope tests - classified OFFICIAL, meets the critical data asset criteria, within your ownership accountabilities.
Record which of the seven purposes each asset supports.
Draw the boundary - only the fields needed for the cross-government purpose form the asset, not the whole system.
If you designate a distribution, designate its source data set too.
Record why each candidate was or was not designated.
checklist: Every asset passes all scope tests
Every asset has at least one purpose
Source data sets designated where a distribution is

stages.name: Confirm ownership
stages.goal: Every designated asset has a named, accountable owner before it is described.
steps: Confirm the owner (data owner or IAO) and steward for each asset with the governance Assign recipe.
Use a shared team contact point for the asset, never a personal inbox.
Record a successor so the metadata survives the owner leaving.
outputs: steward and contact point per asset
checklist: No asset goes forward without a named owner
Contact point is a team route or form

stages.name: Describe
stages.goal: Describe each asset well enough for someone outside your team to find, understand and judge it.
steps: Record the properties in the metadata guidance (see the metadata tab).
Write in plain English; expand acronyms; describe the data, and put usage warnings in usage notes.
Use ISO 8601 dates, IANA media types, and 'unknown' or 'not applicable' rather than blanks.
Model datasets, data services and distributions as the MEM and DCAT do.
Add quality information from the DQAP (see data quality, stage 6).
checklist: Title and description are plain English
Access rights, licence and security classification recorded
Dates in ISO 8601

stages.name: Catalogue and expose
stages.goal: Keep the record in your catalogue in a form others can harvest.
steps: Store each record in the organisation's catalogue, or an asset register where no catalogue exists yet.
Expose records in DCAT so portals and the Discoverability Platform can harvest them.
Make sure every link in a record works from outside your organisation.
Choose catalogue tools against what any catalogue must expose, not a single vendor.
checklist: Records are reachable by harvest, not only by people
No record depends on an internal-only link

stages.name: Report to GDS
stages.goal: Submit an assured return on time.
steps: Prepare the return from catalogue records, not by retyping them.
Collate and assure ALB returns.
Check the return before submission so moderation is about judgement, not formatting.
Submit through the interim template, or the Discoverability Platform when it is live.
checklist: Every asset in the return has an owner, a purpose and current metadata
ALB returns assured by the department

stages.name: Maintain and review
stages.goal: Records stay true.
stages.trigger: Every 12 months, and whenever an asset or its owner changes.
steps: Review every record at least every 12 months.
Update records when the asset changes, and when the owner leaves.
Retire assets that are no longer critical, with a reason.
Feed findings into the governance Assure recipe.
checklist: Every record reviewed in the last 12 months
Owner changes reflected within the month

in_brief: Every critical data asset needs a data quality action plan (DQAP) or an equivalent.
Agree what 'good enough' means with users, test it with rules, and fix the causes of failures.
Publish how good the data is, including what it should not be used for.
before_you_start: A designated asset with a named data owner
Agreement from at least two user teams on what the data is used for
The DQAP template from GOV.UK, or the Data Quality Commons tools
capabilities.name: Data quality
capabilities.question: Is the data good enough for what it is used for, and are we fixing what is not?
capabilities.purpose: Know, prove and improve the quality of each critical data asset through a data quality action plan (DQAP), scored with the government issues framework, reported openly and repeated every cycle.
capabilities.why: Every identified asset must have a DQAP or equivalent (DAM-R06), and existing processes should cover all seven DQAP steps (DAM-R07).
capabilities.method_name: Eight stages over the seven DQAP steps
capabilities.method_intro: Eight stages taken from the Data Quality Commons playbook, which follows the seven steps of the GDS DQAP implementation guide and adds an annual review. Use the Commons for the tools - rule checking, issue scoring and DQAP workbooks; this page is the method and how it joins governance and cataloguing.

stages.name: Identify critical data
stages.goal: Know which data items in each asset matter most.
stages.trigger: The asset is designated and has an owner.
steps: Name the 5 to 15 data items that drive the most important decisions (critical data elements).
Record who uses the data, for what, and who or what it describes.
Log known issues in the DQAP issues log.
checklist: Critical data elements agreed with at least two user teams
You know which groups the data might miss

stages.name: Define rules and targets
stages.goal: Turn 'good enough' into rules a computer can test.
steps: Choose the dimensions that matter - completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity, accuracy.
Write each rule in plain English first, then as a testable rule.
Set targets from the issues framework range for importance times impact.
Store rules as files (a data contract) so they survive a change of tool or supplier.
checklist: Every critical data element has at least one rule
Targets come from user impact, not from what the data already achieves

stages.name: Measure a baseline
stages.goal: Know where you are today.
steps: Profile the data and run every rule; record the date and data version.
Log every failure as an issue with its size and who it affects.
Break results down by group where you lawfully can.
checklist: Results are reproducible
Group differences looked for and recorded

stages.name: Prioritise and set goals
stages.goal: Fix what hurts most first.
steps: Score each issue with the issues framework.
Resolve Critical immediately, High within one cycle, Medium within three and Low within six.
Agree the order with the owner and record accepted risks with a review date.
checklist: Every issue has a priority and a timescale
Issues affecting some groups more than others are not ranked down as 'small'

stages.name: Fix causes at source
stages.goal: Stop problems coming back.
steps: Ask why until you reach the cause - people, process, system, supplier or standard.
Prefer prevention at entry over downstream cleaning.
Put supplier duties and measures into contracts.
Re-run the rule to prove the fix worked.
checklist: Every fix proved by re-running the rule
Any downstream cleaning is recorded and temporary

stages.name: Report openly
stages.goal: Users know how good the data is and what it should not be used for.
steps: Update a plain-English data quality statement - scores, trends, known issues and unsuitable uses.
Publish quality information with the catalogue record (W3C DQV) so it travels with the asset.
Report the status of all assets to the governance board; quality issues enter the issue and risk log.
outputs: Quality metadata on the catalogue record
checklist: Statement says what the data is not fit for
Quality information sits on the catalogue record

stages.name: Repeat and sustain
stages.goal: Quality stays good without heroics.
steps: Run checks automatically on each load or on a fixed cycle.
Track trends and alert when a rule drops below target.
Escalate with the agreed thresholds.
Keep rules, results and the plan in version control.
checklist: Checks run without manual effort
The steward has a named deputy

stages.name: Review every year
stages.goal: Rules and targets still match what users need.
stages.trigger: Every 12 months, on the same date as the catalogue record review.
steps: Review rules, targets and the plan with the owner and users.
Add rules for new uses, including AI.
Retire rules that no longer matter; raise targets that are now easy.
checklist: Reviewed with the catalogue record, not separately
New uses assessed against the AI-ready data guidance

concepts.def: One or more data sets plus, where relevant, the data services used to access them.
A structured collection of data selected and organised for a defined outcome or need. It can be a subset of a larger system.
A controlled means of accessing one or more data sets, such as an API or secure access mechanism.
A specific representation of a data set, for example a CSV file or a feed.
A data asset shared across government where losing access could stop an organisation from fulfilling important functions. 'Essential shared data asset' is the older term it replaced.
Data one organisation gives to another to support an essential process or purpose the receiver is responsible for.
Data one organisation obtains from another to support an essential process or purpose it is responsible for.
One of the seven reasons a critical data asset matters, such as public service delivery or official statistics. Each asset supports at least one.
The conditions an asset must meet to be in scope of the policy: classified OFFICIAL, critical, and within the provider's ownership accountabilities.
Information that describes a data asset so it can be found, understood, validated, reused and shared.
A managed collection of metadata records that helps people and systems find, understand and reuse data assets. It holds descriptions, not the data.
The W3C vocabulary for describing data sets and data services in catalogues, so catalogues can be harvested and searched together.
The UK cross-government model, based on DCAT, for the metadata exchanged about data assets.
The GDS service being scoped to link to departments' own catalogues and make critical data asset metadata discoverable across government.
An organisation's report of its in-scope assets and their metadata to GDS, assured by the department for its ALBs.
A senior leader accountable for the meaning, content, quality and management of a data asset.
The role accountable to the SIRO for protecting the whole information asset. Related to, but not the same as, the data owner.
The role running an asset day to day: standards, access, quality processes and documentation.
The technical expert for the system holding the data: storage, access controls, auditable change and disposal.
A defined set of accountabilities for data. Records name roles, not people.
The choice between keeping the IAO model, adopting the data ownership model, or a hybrid. Each must still meet the mandatory IAO actions.
One of the five repeatable governance activities: Mandate, Frame, Assign, Operate, Assure.
A one-page statement of a governance body's purpose, scope, authority and review cadence.
A running record of governance decisions: what, who, why, when and the review trigger.
A logged, time-bound deviation from policy with an owner and an expiry date. An exception without an expiry is an undocumented policy change.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed. One accountable role per activity.
The plan every identified asset must have, or an equivalent mechanism, for managing its quality across seven steps.
A data item whose quality drives the most important decisions made with the asset.
A measurable aspect of quality. The framework's six are completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy.
The GDS method that scores importance times impact to set targets, and uses the band below target to set priority and time to resolve.
A plain-English summary of an asset's quality, known issues and what it should not be used for.
The W3C vocabulary for publishing quality measurements with a catalogue record.
Quality rules and promises written down as a file that suppliers and users share.
An organisation's capability around data, self-assessed with the government framework.
The person each organisation nominates to coordinate DAM Policy adoption and the return, and to sit on the Working Group.

open_register.reader: The cataloguing method is built from public guidance
open_register.item: The internal Data Cataloguing Playbook v2.6 is not public. The cataloguing stages here are a synthesis of GOV.UK guidance and need checking against it, or replacing with it once cleared.

open_register.reader: How long private feedback is kept is not yet confirmed
open_register.item: Added on 5 November 2026: a private Microsoft Forms route, so people without a GitHub account can give feedback. Set on 8 November 2026: anyone can respond without signing in, names and accounts are not recorded, and every page and test task opens it with the page or task filled in. Contact details are optional and asked for only to reply or send a copy of the answers; Microsoft Forms cannot email an automatic receipt to people who do not sign in, so copies are sent by the maintainers. Still to confirm with the data protection officer: the data controller, how long responses and contact details are kept, and whether the privacy wording on the About page is enough.
Not cleared as official guidance. Clearance, and a move to an official GitHub organisation, are needed before departments are told to rely on it.

No research with real users yet. A research plan with questions, methods, hypotheses and falsification conditions is now published on the Service design page; it needs participants through the Working Group.

open_register.reader: Interoperability requirements are not yet stated
open_register.item: The policy promises minimum interoperability requirements that its body does not state. The Tools and interoperability page proposes open standards for each boundary between tools; these are this portal's synthesis until GDS publishes requirements.

open_register.reader: Proposed metadata terms are not agreed
open_register.item: Four metadata properties in the guidance have no slot in the published MEM. A crosswalk to DCAT and Dublin Core terms is proposed on the cataloguing page (finding F-04) and needs agreement.

open_register.reader: Some dates come from material that is not public
open_register.item: Dates for the rollout phases, returns and support offer come from practitioner material, not a public page. Confirm before external use.
The governance escalation timescales are this playbook's recommendation. Each organisation should set its own.

open_register.reader: Not yet tested with disabled people
open_register.item: Not tested with disabled users or assistive technology users in person; automated checks only.
Data owner versus information asset owner is resolved by the GOV.UK data ownership model (three options). The two maturity models and the remaining glossary conflicts are not resolved here.

open_register.reader: Sector supplements need review by sector experts
open_register.item: All 14 sector themes now have supplements on the Sectors page, signposted from each capability playbook. Each supplement is this portal's synthesis and needs review by subject experts from its sector before organisations rely on it.

Still to do: a ruleset on main that blocks force pushes and deletion and requires the 'Build, check and publish' check.

Still to do: set the default workflow token to read-only and stop GitHub Actions creating or approving pull requests; every workflow already declares the permissions it needs. defects.defect: DQAP was expanded with the wrong middle word, as an 'assurance' plan.
defects.cause: Expansion written from memory, not from the policy text.
defects.check: C-06 bans the wrong expansion anywhere in content or pages.

defects.defect: Evidence was mapped to a policy annex that does not exist.
defects.cause: An assumed reporting template was presented as fact.
defects.check: C-07 bans references to the non-existent annex.

defects.defect: The identification guidance page prints a team email address; copying source text risks putting it on the portal.
defects.cause: Source text carries contact details.
defects.check: C-04 fails the build on any email address in content or published files.

defects.defect: Focusing a tab panel, table region or the graph filled the whole block with the yellow focus colour.
defects.cause: One focus rule targeted every element with a tabindex, including large containers.
defects.check: B-03 focuses each container type and fails if its background becomes the focus colour.

defects.defect: The provenance check passed even when a requirement lost its label, because the source cell's own label satisfied it.
defects.cause: The check looked for a label anywhere in the row, not in the requirement cell.
defects.check: C-08 now inspects the requirement cell alone; its vaccination test removes that label and must fail.

defects.defect: Every page scrolled sideways on 320 and 390 pixel screens.
defects.cause: The colophon barcode had a fixed pixel width.
defects.check: B-02 checks overflow at six widths from 320 to 1920 pixels.

defects.defect: Links in the 'Met by' column were smaller than the 24 pixel target size.
defects.cause: Plain inline links set side by side in a table cell.
defects.check: B-01 runs axe with the WCAG 2.2 AA target-size rule in light and dark modes.

defects.defect: A bulk rename of the portal's owner in the open register also renamed the data owner in the quality escalation table.
defects.cause: A pattern replacement matched role names inside the playbook methods.
defects.check: The build refuses any escalation row that names the portal's service owner; a vaccination test proves it.

defects.defect: Module outcomes and persona goals containing commas were split into fragments such as 'Frame' and 'Assign'.
defects.cause: Unquoted commas inside YAML flow lists.
defects.check: The build refuses list items under three words; a vaccination test proves it.

defects.defect: The external-assets check treated canonical links as remote loads.
defects.cause: The check looked at every link element, not only ones the browser fetches.
defects.check: C-05 now ignores canonical and alternate links; its existing vaccination still fails on a remote script.

defects.defect: The contact form's first error link pointed to a radio button with no id, so it went nowhere.
defects.cause: The error summary is written by script, so the static link check could not see it.
defects.check: B-09 now checks every error summary link resolves to a field.

defects.defect: The health step failed before running because its output folder did not exist on a fresh runner.
defects.cause: The build folder is ignored by git, so it exists locally but not in CI.
defects.check: The workflow creates the folder first; the CI run itself is the check and blocks publishing when it fails.

defects.defect: The health run reported a working GOV.UK organisation page as broken (HTTP 406).
defects.cause: Page checks asked for JSON before HTML, which some GOV.UK pages refuse.
defects.check: A unit test proves page checks ask for HTML first; it fails when the old header is restored.

defects.defect: Stopping all table row headings from wrapping made the library, knowledge and policy pages scroll sideways on phones, and placed feature links too close together.
defects.cause: A global no-wrap rule applied to long titles as well as short identifiers.
defects.check: B-02 (sideways scrolling at six widths) and B-01 (target size) caught it; no-wrap now applies only to identifiers. A second cause was screen-reader-only labels inside wide tables escaping their scroll region; scroll regions are now positioned so they contain them.

defects.defect: On the sectors page at 320 pixels, a filter drop-down sized itself to its longest option and pushed the page sideways.
defects.cause: Flex items in the filter bar kept their minimum content width.
defects.check: B-02 caught it before release; filter controls may now shrink to the screen width.

defects.defect: The new check that every capability shows its explicit, implicit or inferred flag passed even when the flag was removed.
defects.cause: Signpost badges inside the card use the same style, so the check found those instead.
defects.check: C-22 now looks only in the card heading; the vaccination test that exposed it stays in the suite.

defects.defect: The repository's CITATION.cff was published empty in release 1.2.0, so GitHub showed no citation.
defects.cause: A version bump rewrote the file with a pattern that matched nothing and wrote back an empty result; no check looked at the file.
defects.check: C-23 now checks the citation file is complete and names the portal's version; two vaccination tests prove it fails on a blank file and on version drift.

defects.defect: Every workflow run since release 1.2.0 stopped before starting, so releases 1.2.0 to 1.4.0 were not published to GitHub Pages and CodeQL did not run.
defects.cause: The repository only allows actions owned by its owner and pinned to a full commit SHA; the workflows used GitHub's own actions by version tag. Confirmed from the run annotation.
defects.check: Workflows now use plain commands only (git checkout, the runner's Python and Node.js, the CodeQL command-line bundle checked against GitHub's published digest, and a push to the gh-pages branch). C-24 fails the build on any action the policy would refuse.

defects.defect: A single 504 from github.com was recorded as a broken link. The Status page then printed the repository address, which contains the owner's account name, so the personal-details check failed the build and blocked publishing.
defects.cause: The link check treated one server error as proof of a broken link, and the Status page quoted addresses verbatim.
defects.check: The link check retries three times and only counts 404 and 410 as broken; other failures are 'temporarily unavailable'. The Status page names the portal's repository by role. Two tests prove both. CodeQL's bundle download also retries.

defects.found: Review of repository settings after release 1.4
defects.defect: A suggested Jekyll workflow was added and Pages was set to publish from main, which would have published the raw repository files instead of the built portal.
defects.cause: GitHub's Pages settings offer a Jekyll starter workflow by default; nothing in the repository explained that the built site lives on gh-pages.
defects.check: C-24 refused the workflow (unpinned third-party actions) and the build failed safely. The workflow is removed, Pages publishes from gh-pages, and C-25 now fails if any workflow other than the three expected ones appears, or if any workflow publishes from the repository root.

defects.defect: GitHub listed an unrelated account called 'noreply' (location China) as a contributor. It never acted on the repository; four early commits were credited to it.
defects.cause: Automated build sessions committed with GitHub's generic noreply address under the username 'noreply', which GitHub links to the account with that username.
defects.check: C-26 fails the build if the latest commit uses any identity outside an allow-list of the owner, GitHub's bots and the named assistant. Removing the credit on GitHub itself needs those four commits rewritten (OR-17).

defects.found: Owner report on the live portal (version 1.4)
defects.defect: The Playbooks and Frameworks menus opened but showed nothing and could not be clicked, on desktop and inside the More menu on phones.
defects.cause: The top bar hid overflow so it could measure when to fold items into More, and that also cut off the drop-down menus positioned inside it. No browser check opened the menus.
defects.check: The top bar no longer hides overflow; folding still works because it measures scroll width. B-14 opens every grouped menu at 1440 and 390 pixels, checks its first link can be hit and clicked, and follows it; a deliberate break that restores the clipping proves it fails.

defects.defect: The DAMA wheel's segment links had spoken names that did not match their visible labels, and the wheel's area cards pushed the page sideways at 320 pixels.
defects.cause: Segment names were set separately from the visible text, and the card grid had a fixed minimum column width wider than a small phone.
defects.check: B-01 (axe label and name match) and B-02 (sideways scrolling) caught both before release. Segment names now come from the visible label with the detail in a title, and the grid columns shrink to the screen.

defects.defect: Search found nothing on any page and Escape stopped closing it.
defects.cause: The new guided tour script declared a step counter called idx in the same scope as the search index, so the index was replaced by the number 0.
defects.check: B-05 (search finds results and Escape closes it) caught it before release. The tour counter is renamed and commented; B-16 now runs every tour and B-05 runs in the same browser session.

defects.defect: Keyboard shortcut hints in the header failed colour contrast in light mode, and the example configuration on the Use and reuse page pushed the page sideways on phones.
defects.cause: A general style for keyboard keys overrode the header's own style, and the code block had no scrolling of its own.
defects.check: B-01 (axe colour contrast) and B-02 (sideways scrolling) caught both. Key styles now apply only inside the main content and code blocks scroll within themselves.

defects.defect: The new Tools and interoperability page covered the same ground as the Data Quality Commons Catalogues page released earlier the same day, which goes further, with named products, a lock-in checker, an RFI builder and a test script.
defects.cause: The page was written without first looking at what the sister portals already offer.
defects.check: The runbook now starts every new topic with a search of the sister portals. The tooling page keeps what the DAM Policy adds and signposts the Commons and the catalogue; C-34 checks those signposts go only to the sister portals and name them and their status.

defects.defect: The search vaccination crashed instead of running, so the release stopped before publishing.
defects.cause: Every deliberate-break script runs on every page. Adding the compass page, which has none of this portal's own objects, exposed a break script that assumed the search index exists. Only the new compass break was re-run locally after the page was added.
defects.check: Every break script now does nothing where its target is absent, and a test runs each one on an empty page (D-027 in tests). All break modes are run locally before a push that adds a page to the browser checks.

defects.defect: The Status page printed the owner's account name when the health run found a broken link to a sister portal.
defects.cause: The D-019 fix only replaced this portal's own repository address. Version 1.8.3 linked to a Commons page that was committed but not yet published, so the health run quoted the Commons address in full.
defects.check: Every address in the owner's account or Pages site is now named by what it is (this portal, the Commons, the catalogue), keeping the page name. A test feeds the Status page sister-portal problems and runs C-17 on it.

defects.defect: Re-running the icon vendoring script would have dropped 11 icons the site uses, including the compass and tools page icons.
defects.cause: Icons added in versions 1.8.0 to 1.8.2 were written into site_src/icons.json directly, not added to the script's list.
defects.check: The script's list now covers every icon, and a test fails if any icon the site uses is missing from it.

defects.defect: The Open data page said '1 files' and offered downloads for only a few datasets, because it was built before the data files were written.
defects.cause: The page filters each dataset's files by whether they exist, and the data files are written after the pages.
defects.check: The page is built again after the data files are written. C-28 now fails if any file in the catalogue has no download link on the Open data page.

defects.defect: What's new showed raw Markdown backticks around file names, such as `research.html`.
defects.cause: Changelog lines were escaped as plain text.
defects.check: Backticks are shown as code on What's new and in the releases feed. C-37 fails if a backtick appears in the visible text of What's new.

defects.defect: The private Microsoft feedback form opened blank from every page and test task, so a response could not be traced to the page or task it was about, and the portal said the form might ask people to sign in when it does not.
defects.cause: Links used the bare form address, pre-filled answers were switched off in Microsoft Forms, and the form note was written before the response setting was chosen.
defects.check: Pre-filled answers are on, and every link is built with the page or task filled in. C-33 now fails if any page lacks a link with that page filled in, if any test task is not filled in as task feedback, if a pre-fill question id is malformed, if a form link goes elsewhere or if the privacy wording is missing from About; the build rejects an unknown topic.

defects.defect: A data dictionary format with a comma in it was split into a stray key with no value, so the title's format lost its second half without any error.
defects.cause: Unquoted commas inside a YAML flow mapping start a new key.
defects.check: The build now rejects any dictionary entry with unexpected or empty keys and says to quote values that contain a comma; a test proves it.

defects.defect: Every compass link to DCAT-AP-UK, and the DAM pages' Related link to it, returned 404 after the profile's site moved from dcat-uk-ap to dcat-ap-uk.
defects.cause: Links into the other portals were only checked by hand; nothing re-read them when a portal changed.
defects.check: tools/compass_sync.py reads every compass link into the other portals daily in CI, hides any that are gone, and opens a compass-sync issue; tests prove it finds a gone page and a missing anchor and treats an unreachable portal as unchecked.

defects.defect: Opening the compass with no address jumped down the page to the first tab and outlined it.
defects.cause: The pathway wrote the address while the page was still loading, so the browser then scrolled to that fragment and focused it.
defects.check: The compass never writes the address while loading or to say what is already shown. C-35 checks the guard and B-17 checks that the page stays at the top with an empty address.

defects.defect: Five template fields had been split in two since they were written, for example 'Ownership option (IAO' and 'data owner or hybrid)' in the ownership register, so downloads and the Library showed broken fields and inflated field counts.
defects.cause: The same as D-033: unquoted commas in YAML flow lists start a new item.
defects.check: Fields are quoted, and the build rejects any template field whose brackets do not balance; a test proves it. The C-39 health check also first missed a removed step because the reference titles repeat the words; it now looks for the steps themselves.

defects.defect: The menu links to the Governance, Cataloguing and Quality playbooks showed an empty tooltip on every page.
defects.cause: Menu tooltips come from page descriptions, and the three playbook pages had none, so the grouped menu fell back to empty text.
defects.check: Menu tooltips now fall back to the capability's purpose. C-40 fails any page with an empty tooltip; a test proves it.

defects.defect: The build failed twice before any check ran, because the runner could not reach Ubuntu's package mirror while installing the browser's system packages.
defects.cause: One attempt, with no retry or fallback, at a step that depends on an outside mirror.
defects.check: The workflow retries three times a minute apart, each attempt capped at 10 minutes after one ran for over 90 minutes without finishing, then installs the browser alone; the browser checks still fail if it cannot start. C-25 fails if the retry or the time limits go; two tests prove it.

defects.defect: Six of the nine professions on the By profession tab showed no icon.
defects.cause: The compass icon set was built only from icons named in the page template and a few lists; icons named only in the data, such as each profession's, were left out, so the browser drew empty symbols.
defects.check: The build now takes every icon the data names. C-35 fails if any icon named in the data or the page has no symbol, and B-17 checks every profession card shows a drawn icon.

defects.defect: Defect numbers D-034 and D-035 were each used twice, by two sessions working at the same time.
defects.cause: Defect ids were not checked for uniqueness, and sessions pick the next number from their own copy.
defects.check: The build now rejects a duplicate defect id. The compass entries were renumbered D-037 and D-038; the earlier D-034 and D-035 keep their numbers.

defects.defect: The compass's own self-check said the Repos Asset Catalogue facts were 36 days old, and one figure in them (25,981 projects) could no longer be reproduced from that catalogue's data.
defects.cause: The 30-day freshness test ran only in the browser; nothing in CI or the daily sync looked at it.
defects.check: The daily sync now lists portal facts older than 30 days and opens an issue for them. The facts were rechecked against the catalogue's repository and the unreproducible figure replaced with its README's own wording.

defects.defect: The DAMA drill-down assessment still said eight areas had no activities and that data architecture had no steps, measures or standards, after the Knowledge areas page had added them.
defects.cause: Two pieces of work changed the same area in parallel; the assessment was written as text, with nothing tying it to the activities it describes.
defects.check: C-40 now fails if the assessment says areas have no activities, or that data architecture has no steps, measures or standards, while the Knowledge areas content has them. A test proves it.

defects.defect: The health run reported the EU Data Act link on EUR-Lex as broken (404), although the address is the one the European Commission itself publishes. Locally the same check passed it with a 202, for a made-up law as well as the real one.
defects.cause: EUR-Lex answers automated checks with an AWS WAF bot challenge instead of the page: 202 to some clients, 404 to others. The checker read the status alone, so a challenge counted as ok or as broken depending on the runner, and never as unchecked.
defects.check: A response carrying a bot challenge header (x-amzn-waf-action or cf-mitigated), or a 202, is now blocked: listed for a person to check, not counted as ok or broken. Three tests prove a challenge is blocked whether it comes as 202 or 404, and that a plain 404 is still broken.

adversarial.challenge: Another portal adds to the scatter it claims to fix. Practitioners already describe the playbooks as 'published, none joined'.
adversarial.answer: It holds no second copy of anything with a master elsewhere. GOV.UK pages, the MEM and the Data Quality Commons are linked, not copied. What it adds is the join: the requirements matrix, one role model and the interlocks.

adversarial.challenge: Readers will mistake this playbook's stage sequences for GOV.UK requirements.
adversarial.answer: Every requirement carries its source and strength (must, should, method, gap); stages are labelled as synthesis; provenance badges sit on every fact.

adversarial.challenge: Base rate: catalogue programmes commonly stall on adoption rather than on tooling (K, a lead not a measured fact).
adversarial.answer: The method puts ownership before description and reporting from catalogue records, so effort lands where adoption fails. Whether that is enough is untested (OR-04).

adversarial.challenge: It is built before learning from users.
adversarial.answer: Named as a risk (OR-04). The journeys say they are assumed needs.

adversarial.challenge: It is hosted outside an official organisation and is not cleared.
adversarial.answer: Stated on every page and in OR-03. The content is OGL and the code MIT, so it can move to an official organisation unchanged.

personas.title: Data owner
personas.summary: You are the senior leader accountable for the meaning, content, quality and management of one or more critical data assets.
personas.context: Data ownership is one of several responsibilities. You make decisions and sign off; others do the day-to-day work.
goals: Understand exactly what you are accountable for
Make decisions quickly with the right evidence
Name a successor so the asset is never orphaned

needs.need: a clear list of the decisions that are mine
needs.so: I can sign off with confidence

needs.need: to see how good my data is and what it should not be used for
needs.so: I can accept or reject risks knowingly

pains: Unclear difference between data owner and information asset owner
Asked to sign things without the context
design_for: Uses screen magnification at 200 per cent
personas.success: You can explain your assets' purpose, quality and risks, and your successor is named.

tasks.label: Accept the role and name a successor

personas.title: Data steward
personas.summary: You run critical data assets day to day - their standards, access, metadata and quality processes.
personas.context: You do the detailed work and keep the records current. You need step-by-step methods and templates.
goals: Keep the catalogue record and the DQAP current without heroics
Find problems before users do
Hand over cleanly when you move on

needs.so: I can do the work consistently across assets

needs.need: one place to record each fact once
needs.so: the catalogue, the DQAP and the register always agree

pains: The same owner and review date recorded in three places
Quality rules kept only in one tool
design_for: Uses a screen reader for long documents
personas.success: Every asset you steward has a current record, rules with targets, and a quality statement users understand.

personas.title: Catalogue manager or data custodian
personas.summary: You run the catalogue and the systems behind it, so records can be found, harvested and kept accurate.
personas.context: You work with tools and standards. You need to know what any catalogue must expose, whatever the product.
goals: Records that machines can harvest, not only people
Conform to the cross-government metadata standard
Avoid lock-in to one product

needs.need: the exact metadata properties and how they map to the standard
to know what the Discoverability Platform will expect
needs.so: we do not rebuild the feed later

pains: Guidance and model do not list the same properties
Internal-only links break outside the organisation
personas.success: Every critical data asset record is complete, conforms to the standard and can be harvested as DCAT.

personas.title: Data quality lead or analyst
personas.summary: You bring methods and tools for measuring and improving quality across many assets.
personas.context: You support several stewards. You need a consistent scoring method and tools that work without installing anything.
goals: Score issues the same way across assets
Automate measurement across assets
Show quality fairly for every group the data describes

needs.need: the government scoring method and tools that apply it
checks that break results down by group
needs.so: poor quality for some people is not averaged away

design_for: Colour-blind, so charts must not rely on colour alone
personas.success: Every critical data asset has scored issues, automated checks and quality reported by group where lawful.

personas.title: Programme or project lead
personas.summary: You lead a medium or large change programme or project that creates, changes, migrates or retires critical data assets.
personas.context: Your programme has its own governance, gates, budget and suppliers. Data asset management can feel like someone else's job until a gate review, a migration or handover exposes the gaps.
goals: Pass assurance gates without late data surprises
Hand over assets with owners and quality plans in place
Avoid creating the next legacy system

needs.need: to know which DAM duties apply to my programme and when
needs.so: they are planned and funded from the business case

needs.need: clear data roles inside my programme team
needs.so: nobody assumes someone else is doing it

pains: Data owners sit outside the programme and are hard to reach
Migration quality problems surface only at cutover
design_for: Reads on the move between meetings
Needs a one-page view to share with the programme board
personas.success: Every critical asset the programme touches has an owner, a catalogue entry and a quality plan before the programme closes.

tasks.label: Confirm data owners for every asset in scope of the programme
List the critical assets the programme creates, changes or retires
Agree quality rules and targets with owners before build
Show DAM evidence at each gate review
Hand over the DQAP and ownership to business as usual

modules.title: The DAM Policy - what it asks of you
outcomes: Explain who the policy applies to and what is in scope
Name the core duties: identify and catalogue assets, report them, name an owner and manage quality
Find the requirement behind any step in these playbooks

activities.text: Read the summary of who the policy applies to and what is in scope.
Scan the requirements table. Filter it to 'must' to see the core duties.
Note which of the reporting dates applies to your organisation first.
Which of the three capabilities is least developed in your organisation today?

check.q: Which organisations must follow the policy?
options: UK government departments and their arm's length bodies
Only departments that publish open data
check.why: It applies to UK government departments and their ALBs. It is optional for public corporations and does not apply to councils.

check.q: What must every identified data asset have?
options: A named data owner and a DQAP or equivalent
check.why: The policy requires a named data owner and a data quality action plan, or an equivalent mechanism, for every identified asset.

modules.title: Roles and accountability
outcomes: Describe the data owner, data steward and data custodian roles
Explain how the data owner relates to the information asset owner
Choose between the three ownership options

activities.text: Read the role model shared by all three playbooks.
Read the Assign recipe and its checklist.
List your critical data assets and the role that should own each one.
Does every owner in your list have a named successor?

check.q: Which role is accountable for an asset's meaning, content and quality?
check.why: The data owner is the senior leader accountable. The steward runs the asset day to day; the custodian runs the technical system.

check.q: What must happen when a data owner leaves?
options: A successor is ready and the metadata is updated
check.why: The guidance asks you to tell the coordinating team, have a successor ready and update the metadata.

modules.title: Setting up governance with five recipes
outcomes: Run the Mandate, Frame, Assign, Operate and Assure recipes in order
Set up a decision log and an exception register
Collect evidence continuously for the GDS return

activities.text: Work through the five recipes step by step.
Draft a one-page charter using the template.
Set up a decision log and an exception register using the templates.
Where will your evidence folder live, and who keeps it current?

check.q: What makes an exception different from a policy change?
options: It has an owner and an expiry date
It is approved by the minister
check.why: An exception is time-bound with an owner and an expiry date. Without an expiry it is an undocumented policy change.

check.q: When should you assemble evidence for the return?
options: In the month before the deadline
check.why: Collecting evidence each time a decision is logged turns the return into collation rather than reconstruction.

modules.title: Finding and designating critical data assets
outcomes: Build a candidate list from existing registers
Apply the scope tests and the seven purposes
Draw an asset's boundary and record why

activities.text: Read stages 1 to 3 of the cataloguing method.
Start a candidate log using the designation template.
For one candidate, record which of the seven purposes it supports.
Have you looked at data you acquire from others, not only data you provide?

check.q: If you designate a distribution of a data set, what else should you designate?
check.why: The guidance asks you to designate the source data set as well.

check.q: Which of these is one of the seven purposes?
check.why: Official statistics is one of the seven. The statistics themselves are not designated, only the data used to produce them.

modules.title: Describing assets with metadata others can use
outcomes: Record the metadata properties in the GOV.UK guidance
Write titles and descriptions in plain English
Map properties to the Metadata Exchange Model

activities.text: Read the metadata properties and how to record each one.
Complete a catalogue record for one asset using the template.
Ask someone outside your team to read the record and say what the data is for.
Which properties did you have to mark 'unknown'? Who could supply them?

check.q: How should you record a date in a catalogue record?
options: As written in the source system
check.why: The guidance asks for ISO 8601, for example 2020-07-14.

check.q: What should you put when a property has no value?
check.why: Use 'unknown' or 'not applicable' rather than leaving a blank.

modules.title: Cataloguing, harvesting and reporting to GDS
outcomes: Expose records so others can harvest them
Produce the return from catalogue records
Plan the annual review

activities.text: Read stages 6 to 8 of the cataloguing method.
Check that every link in one record works from outside your network.
Put the annual review date in the same diary entry as the DQAP review.

check.q: How often must metadata be reviewed?
check.why: The policy asks for metadata to be maintained and reviewed annually.

check.q: Who assures the returns of arm's length bodies?
check.why: Departments coordinate and assure the returns of their ALBs.

modules.title: Data quality foundations
outcomes: Name the five principles and six dimensions of the Government Data Quality Framework
Explain what a DQAP is for
Recognise when quality differs between groups of people

activities.text: Read the principles and dimensions.
Read the overview of the quality playbook.
Which dimension matters most for your most important decision?

check.q: Which is one of the six dimensions?
check.why: The six are completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy.

check.q: Why break quality results down by group?
options: So poor quality for some people is not averaged away
Because the law always requires it
check.why: An average can hide poor quality for some groups, which can exclude them from services.

modules.title: Building a DQAP and scoring issues
outcomes: Write rules with targets from the issues framework
Measure a baseline and log issues
Prioritise issues and set resolution dates

activities.text: Work through the eight quality stages step by step.
Write three rules for one critical data element using the template.
Score an issue with the issues framework calculator.
Which issue would you fix at source rather than clean downstream?

check.q: How does the issues framework set a rule's target range?
options: From what the data already achieves
From importance of purpose times impact
From the size of the data set
check.why: Importance of purpose multiplied by impact gives a combined score, which sets the target range.

check.q: In the framework's example timescales, when is a critical issue resolved?
check.why: The framework's example gives Critical as immediate; High, Medium and Low within 1, 3 and 6 measurements.

modules.title: Running the three capabilities as one yearly cycle
outcomes: Use the hand-offs so each fact is recorded once
Plan one annual review per asset
Feed assurance lessons into the next mandate

activities.text: Read the hand-offs between the capabilities.
Read the joined-up year.
Pick one asset and check the owner is the same in the register, the record and the DQAP.

check.q: Where should the owner and successor for an asset be recorded first?
options: In the ownership register, then reused
check.why: The ownership register is the source; the catalogue record and the DQAP reuse it (IL-01, IL-02).

modules.title: Inclusive data practice
outcomes: Apply equality and inclusion checks in each capability
Make data quality statements and records accessible
Involve people the data describes

activities.text: Read the inclusion checks for each capability.
Run the inclusion questions against one of your assets.
Whose voice is missing when you decide what 'good enough' means?

check.q: Which duty asks public bodies to consider equality in their work?
options: The Statistics and Registration Service Act
check.why: The public sector equality duty in the Equality Act 2010 applies to public authorities in their functions.

modules.title: Embedding the policy in delivery and change
outcomes: Name the capabilities the policy relies on but does not state
Build DAM checkpoints into a business case and an assurance plan
Plan a legacy exit and a handover to business as usual

activities.text: Read what the policy leaves to you and the life cycle overlay.
Take one programme you know and tick the actions that already happen, then list the gaps.
Run the self-assessment for your organisation and download the result.
Which critical asset would be left without an owner if its project closed tomorrow?

check.q: Which guidance makes a register of data assets its second principle?
check.why: The GOV.UK guidance on managing legacy technology asks organisations to build a complete and accurate register of their data assets.

check.q: How does the capability model flag a need the DAM Policy text does not state at all?
check.why: Inferred means the need is not in the text and comes from good practice and adjacent rulebooks.

duties.name: Public sector equality duty (Equality Act 2010)
duties.text: Have due regard to eliminating discrimination, advancing equality of opportunity and fostering good relations, across the protected characteristics.

duties.name: Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018
duties.text: Websites and documents you publish, including data quality statements and catalogue pages, must meet accessibility requirements.

duties.name: UK GDPR accuracy principle
duties.text: Personal data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. Inaccuracy can fall harder on some groups.

duties.name: Welsh Language Standards and devolved duties
duties.text: Where your organisation is subject to them, statements and records meant for the public must meet them.

items: Include equality considerations in the charter and the board's terms of reference
Make sure owners and stewards have accessible training and materials
Record decisions that affect groups differently, with the equality analysis behind them
Invite representatives of people the data describes when the board sets priorities
Write titles and descriptions in plain English and expand acronyms
Record known gaps in coverage - people, places or periods the data misses
Check address, name and identifier fields work for all four UK nations and overseas
Make sure catalogue pages and records meet accessibility requirements
Break quality results down by group where you lawfully can
Record poorer quality for a group as its own issue, so it is not averaged away
Fix forms that force wrong answers, such as no 'prefer not to say' or one-line names
Test quality statements with people outside the data team, and offer accessible formats

questions: Does the data cover everyone it should? Compare its coverage with an independent count by group and place.
Is missing or wrong data worse for some groups?
Can people describe themselves accurately in the forms and systems that create the data?
Do rules and records work for all four UK nations, and for Welsh language users where required?
Are the outputs (records, statements, reports) accessible and in plain English?
Have people the data describes, or their representatives, had a say?
If the data feeds automated decisions or AI, has bias been assessed?
portal: Plain English, short sections, sentence case and a summary at the top of every page
Works with a keyboard, screen readers and magnification; tested automatically against WCAG 2.2 AA
Light and dark modes, larger text and wider line spacing, chosen in display options
No information conveyed by colour alone; every chart and graph has a table equivalent
Pages still work with scripts turned off; progress tracking is an optional extra
Progress is kept only in your own browser; nothing about you is collected

sectors: Department of Health and Social Care ALBs
domain_depth.why: Health bodies hold many critical data assets about people, often with legal duties beyond the DAM Policy. Quality failures here fall hardest on people who already face health inequalities.
needed: Map data owner and steward roles to Caldicott guardians, SIROs and clinical safety officers
Quality rules for clinical coding (SNOMED CT, ICD-10, OPCS-4) and NHS number validity
Read-across to the NHS Data Security and Protection Toolkit and the national data opt-out
A worked example of a DQAP for a patient-level data set
leads: DCB0129 and DCB0160 clinical safety standards

domain_depth.theme: Adult and children's social care data
sectors: Department of Health and Social Care
domain_depth.why: Social care data flows from councils to central government, so critical data assets depend on systems outside the policy's scope, often legacy case management systems.
needed: Guidance for assets acquired from councils that are not bound by the policy
Quality rules for client level data returns and outcomes frameworks
Handling legacy system exports and cross-boundary records
leads: Adult social care client level data

domain_depth.why: The metadata guidance names GEMINI for geospatial data, and most critical data assets carry an address or location that needs a shared identifier.
needed: GEMINI metadata alongside the core properties, with a crosswalk
Rules for UPRN and USRN validity and match rates
Positional and thematic accuracy checks (ISO 19157)
Q-FAIR quality ratings in catalogue records

domain_depth.why: Official statistics is one of the seven purposes. The data used to produce statistics is designated, and its quality is also judged under the Code of Practice for Statistics.
needed: Read-across between the DQAP and quality assurance of administrative data (QAAD)
Statistical metadata (SDMX) alongside DCAT
How to report quality once for both the DAM return and statistical quality reports

domain_depth.why: Critical data assets are defined by being shared. Owners need to know the legal basis for each flow, which changed with the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
needed: A legal gateway field and decision record in the governance templates
Read-across to data sharing agreements and the ICO data sharing code
What the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 changes for owners
leads: Digital Economy Act 2017 data sharing powers
ICO data sharing code of practice

sectors: All departments using data for AI or automated decision support
domain_depth.why: The annual review asks whether new uses include AI. Owners need criteria, not just a prompt.
needed: An AI-readiness checklist mapped to quality dimensions and catalogue fields
When an algorithmic transparency record is needed
Bias and representativeness rules for training data
leads: GDS guidelines on making government datasets ready for AI
ISO/IEC 5259 data quality for analytics and machine learning

domain_depth.theme: Tax, benefits and fraud and error
domain_depth.why: Fraud and error is one of the seven purposes. These assets combine high volume, personal data and decisions about people.
needed: Quality rules for identity matching and false positives
Governance for data used in fraud detection, including review of automated flags

domain_depth.why: Only OFFICIAL assets are in scope, and law enforcement processing follows Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018. Owners need to know where the line falls.
needed: How to describe an asset whose metadata is itself sensitive
Handling markings in catalogue records
Roles where vetting applies

domain_depth.theme: Person, identity and vulnerability data standards
sectors: All departments holding data about people
domain_depth.why: Draft cross-government standards for person and vulnerability data affect how assets are described and checked.
needed: Link catalogue fields and quality rules to the person data standard when it is published
Inclusive rules for names, sex and gender questions and 'prefer not to say' options

domain_depth.why: Code lists and authoritative identifiers make assets interoperable, but the policy does not yet list which to use (OR-05).
needed: A register of recommended identifiers and code lists by domain
Ownership patterns for shared reference data

sectors: All departments; knowledge and information management teams
domain_depth.why: The Frame recipe lists retention and disposal, but owners need the link between data assets and records management schedules.
needed: Retention fields in the ownership register
Read-across to The National Archives guidance
leads: The National Archives information management guidance

domain_depth.why: The policy does not bind them, but many critical data assets flow to or from them. Pan-UK assets need each nation's view.
needed: A four-nations view of equivalent policies and standards
Bilingual (Welsh) catalogue and quality statement guidance where it applies
Voluntary adoption route for councils

domain_depth.why: Large holders of shared spatial and monitoring data, with sensor and time-series quality issues the core rules do not cover.
needed: Timeliness and completeness rules for sensor and time-series data
Metadata aligned with INSPIRE

sectors: All departments; design authorities and data architects
domain_depth.why: Raised by a pilot team (Project Compass, 11 November 2026): critical data assets need their entities, relationships and authoritative sources described, and relationship diagrams linked to the catalogue and data dictionary.
needed: An entity and relationship list linked to catalogue records
A relationship diagram produced from the list, in an open text format
leads: DAMA-DMBOK data architecture and data modelling and design knowledge areas

sectors: Department for Education and its ALBs
domain_depth.why: Pupil and learner records are long-lived and linked across services.
needed: Quality rules for unique pupil and learner identifiers
Coverage checks across school types and nations

standards.name: Self-describing
standards.how: Artefact meta tags, JSON-LD on every page, DCAT catalogue, SKOS vocabulary, sitemap

standards.name: Self-testing
standards.how: Static and browser checks on every change; each check proved to fail on a deliberate break; release blocked on failure

standards.name: Self-degrading
standards.how: Declared shed order in app.js; every page readable with scripts off (browser check B-07)

standards.name: Self-updating
standards.how: Weekly health run re-checks every source date through the GOV.UK Content API and every external link, and reports changes on the Status page

standards.name: Self-reviewing
standards.how: Weekly health run fails when the review date has passed and opens an issue

standards.name: Self-reporting
standards.how: status.json and the Status page publish health, coverage and open problems; failures open a GitHub issue

standards.name: Self-limiting
standards.how: Automation only reads, builds and opens issues. A person merges, tags releases and changes settings

standards.name: Self-securing
standards.how: Content Security Policy, CodeQL, Dependabot alerts and secret scanning. Branch protection to be switched on by the repository owner

standards.name: Self-costing
standards.how: Health run measures page weight against a 1.5 MB per page envelope; CI minutes are free for public repositories

standards.name: Self-reconciling
standards.how: Build refuses broken references between requirements, steps, roles, modules and sources; counts are computed, never typed

standards.name: Self-documenting
standards.how: What's new page generated from the changelog; release notes generated by GitHub releases

standards.name: Self-profiling
standards.how: Page weight measured; no measurement of where users wait, because no analytics are collected

standards.name: Self-explaining
standards.how: Search ranking rule and progress rules explained on the About page; every fact carries a provenance label

standards.name: Self-calibrating
standards.how: Learning time estimates are not yet compared with real completion times

standards.name: Architecture decisions recorded
standards.how: docs/adr

standards.name: Protected main branch with review
standards.how: Pull request template and CODEOWNERS in place; the owner must switch on branch protection

standards.name: Negative tests prove each check
standards.how: tests/test_checks.py and browser vaccinations in CI

standards.name: Accessibility tested automatically
standards.how: axe-core, WCAG 2.2 AA, light and dark, six widths

standards.name: Dependencies pinned and updated on a clock
standards.how: Exact pins; Dependabot weekly; GitHub dependency graph provides the bill of materials

standards.name: Continuous integration on every change
standards.how: Build, check and publish workflow

standards.name: Release train and checklist
standards.how: Tag-triggered release workflow and the release checklist in docs/RUNBOOK.md

standards.name: Scheduled health run with alert
standards.how: Weekly health workflow; failures open or update a labelled issue

standards.name: Runbooks
standards.how: docs/RUNBOOK.md

standards.name: No single person or account the portal depends on
standards.how: Hosted on one personal account; move to an official organisation (OR-03)

standards.name: Static-first delivery
standards.how: Static pages on GitHub Pages; no server code

standards.name: Personal data kept out
standards.how: No analytics, no cookies; progress stays in the browser; the contact form warns against personal data

standards.name: Algorithmic transparency
standards.how: Not applicable: no automated decisions about people. Recorded here as the decision

standards.name: Service Standard self-assessment
standards.how: Self-assessment against all 14 points on the Service design page; no service assessment yet

standards.name: Horizon scanning
standards.how: Weekly source checks flag changed GOV.UK guidance for review

findings.title: Issues framework Table 4 contradicts its own rule for a 97.5% target
findings.detail: The framework says the High band starts halfway between the Middle band start and the target. For a 97.5% target the Middle band starts at 95%, so the High band should start at 96.25%. Table 4 shows 96.75%. The other four rows follow the rule.
findings.action: This portal follows the stated rule. Raise with the GDS data quality team; tracked as a repository issue.
