supplements.title: Health and care data
supplements.summary: For critical data assets that hold patient-level or care records. Adds the health roles, duties and coding standards the core playbooks do not cover.
gov: Map the data owner and steward to the Caldicott Guardian, the SIRO and, for health IT, the clinical safety officer. Record who holds each role for every asset.
Record the legal basis for each use, the common law duty of confidentiality position and whether the national data opt-out applies.
Check the organisation's latest Data Security and Protection Toolkit assessment covers the systems that hold the asset.
Apply the Caldicott principles when deciding what each user of the asset needs: the minimum necessary, justified for each purpose.
Record the clinical terminology and exchange standards the asset follows, such as SNOMED CT, dm+d and HL7 FHIR UK Core, in conformsTo, so the MEM record points to the sector standard.
Where a health IT system holds the asset, record its clinical safety position: DCB0129 for the supplier and DCB0160 for the organisation that deploys it.

If confidential patient information is used without consent, record the legal basis that sets aside the duty of confidentiality, such as section 251 support, separately from the data protection lawful basis.
If software or AI that uses the asset has a medical purpose, check whether it is a medical device under the Medical Devices Regulations 2002, using the MHRA's guidance.

If NHS health and social care data in the asset is used for research or analysis beyond direct care, give access through a secure data environment, as DHSC's secure data environment policy guidelines require, and record which environment in the catalogue record.

cat.rule: The lawful basis and, for health data, the special category condition
Whether the national data opt-out has been applied to this distribution (yes, no or not applicable)
Identifiable, pseudonymised or anonymised, and the method used
The NHS data set or Data Dictionary standard the data follows

rules.rule: NHS number is recorded
NHS number is 10 digits with a valid modulus 11 check digit
Date of birth is not in the future
Provider organisation code is in ODS format
Primary diagnosis is in ICD-10 code format
Ethnic category is not unknown or not stated
NHS number completeness does not differ by more than 5 points between ethnic groups

identifiers.name: NHS number
identifiers.format: 10 digits; the last is a modulus 11 check digit

identifiers.name: ODS code
identifiers.format: 3 to 6 letters and digits identifying an NHS or care organisation

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: an outpatient activity extract shared with a central department. Critical data elements are NHS number, provider code, attendance date and primary diagnosis. Baseline shows NHS number completeness of 97% overall but 91% for one ethnic group; HLT-07 records that as its own issue so it is not averaged away.
risks: Pseudonymised data is still personal data; access controls and agreements still apply.
Opt-outs and local suppression can bias coverage for some groups; check coverage against an independent count.
Clinical codes can be valid in format but wrong in meaning; format checks do not replace clinical coding audit.
checklist: Caldicott Guardian, SIRO and clinical safety officer roles are recorded for the asset
Legal basis, confidentiality position and opt-out status are recorded on the catalogue record
NHS number validity and completeness rules are in the DQAP
Quality is broken down by ethnic group where lawful
Access for research and analysis goes through a secure data environment, recorded on the catalogue record

supplements.title: Adult and children's social care data
supplements.summary: For assets built from council returns, such as adult social care client level data and children's social care census returns, where the source systems sit outside the policy's scope.
gov: Record which councils supply the data and that they are not bound by the DAM Policy; agree quality expectations through the collection's own guidance.
Name the owner for the national asset and a contact route for suppliers, not individuals.
Record changes to collection specifications as decisions, because they change what the asset means.

cat.rule: The councils and nations covered, using GSS codes
The submission cycle, for example quarterly
The collection specification and its version

rules.rule: Supplying council is a valid GSS code
NHS number is valid where present, so care and health records can be linked
Event dates are not in the future
Each council's latest submission is no more than one quarter and 30 days old
Each event is recorded once for each person

identifiers.name: GSS code
identifiers.format: One letter (E, K, L, M, N, S or W) followed by 8 digits

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a quarterly client level data asset. SOC-04 shows two councils have not submitted for two quarters; the owner records the gap in the quality statement rather than imputing it.
risks: Councils use different case management systems, so the same field can be captured differently.
Late or missing submissions make national figures look better or worse than they are.
Linking to health data depends on NHS number quality in council systems.
checklist: Supplying organisations and the collection specification are recorded
Timeliness by supplier is measured and reported
NHS number validity is checked where linkage is planned

supplements.title: Geospatial and address data
supplements.summary: For assets that hold addresses, coordinates or map geometry. Adds geospatial metadata, open identifiers and positional quality.
gov: Record the licence for any third-party geospatial data the asset depends on, and who may use derived data.
Use the open identifiers for property and street (UPRN and USRN) as the join between assets.
Apply the Geospatial Commission's guidance on ethical use of location data when location could identify people.

cat.rule: The area covered, by GSS code or bounding box
The coordinate reference system, for example British National Grid (EPSG:27700)
How the geometry was captured and processed
UK GEMINI where the asset is geospatial

rules.rule: UPRN is recorded
UPRN is 1 to 12 digits
Postcode is in Royal Mail format
Easting is within the British National Grid range
Northing is within the British National Grid range
Area code is a GSS code

identifiers.name: UPRN
identifiers.format: Unique property reference number, up to 12 digits

identifiers.name: USRN
identifiers.format: Unique street reference number, up to 8 digits

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a register of public buildings. GEO-02 passes but 6% of UPRNs do not match the address base used by the receiving department; the owner logs a consistency issue and agrees a match-rate target.
risks: A valid UPRN format does not prove the property exists or is the right one; check match rates against the authoritative address base.
Coordinates in mixed reference systems silently misplace features.
Small-area location data can identify people even when names are removed.
checklist: UPRN and USRN are used as join keys where they exist
The coordinate reference system and lineage are on the catalogue record
Positional checks and match rates are in the DQAP
Licences for third-party geospatial inputs are recorded

supplements.title: Official statistics and administrative sources
supplements.summary: For assets used to produce official statistics. Joins the DQAP to quality assurance of administrative data, so quality is reported once for both purposes.
gov: Record the statistics produced from the asset and the producer responsible for them.
Agree with the statistics producer how supplier changes are communicated before they happen.
Use the DQAP as evidence for the assurance level set under quality assurance of administrative data.

cat.rule: The official statistics that use the asset
SDMX structure or statistical classification used, where one applies

rules.rule: Reference period is complete with no missing months
Monthly totals are not implausible outliers
Area codes are valid GSS codes
Every measure column names its unit

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: an administrative benefits extract used for quarterly statistics. STA-02 flags a sudden fall in one month that turns out to be a supplier system change; it is logged as a known issue in both the DQAP and the statistical release.
risks: Operational changes in the supplier's system can look like real-world change.
Two quality reports for the same data drift apart unless one feeds the other.
checklist: Statistics that depend on the asset are recorded on the catalogue record
A supplier change notice process is agreed
DQAP results are used as evidence for administrative data quality assurance

supplements.title: Data sharing and legal gateways
supplements.summary: For every critical data asset that includes personal data, because critical data assets are defined by being shared. Adds a legal gateway record to the governance and catalogue records.
gov: Keep a sharing decision record for each flow: purpose, lawful basis, any special category condition, legal power or gateway, DPIA reference, agreement reference and review date.
Check each flow against the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 changes to UK GDPR at the next review.
Use a data sharing agreement for routine sharing, as the ICO code recommends, even where it is not mandatory.
Name the owner on both sides of every flow, by role.
If the flow uses a Part 5 power in the Digital Economy Act 2017, check the agreement is on the published register.
Record the agreement with the data sharing agreement template (T-GOV-6), and name the legal gateway in it and in the catalogue record.

cat.rule: Restricted, with the agreement reference
The statutory power or legal basis for the flow
Conditions on onward sharing and use

rules.rule: Every shared extract carries the agreement reference
Extracts arrive on the agreed schedule
Only the columns in the agreement are present

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a monthly flow of eligibility data between two departments. The sharing decision record names the gateway, the DPIA and the agreement; SHR-03 fails when an extra free-text column appears, which is fixed at source before the next transfer.
risks: Extra fields creep into extracts over time, beyond what the agreement allows.
Lawful basis recorded once at the start of a flow can go out of date when the law or the purpose changes.
checklist: A sharing decision record exists for each flow, with a review date
Agreement references appear on the catalogue record and in each extract
Flows were reviewed against the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 changes

supplements.title: AI-ready data
supplements.summary: For assets used, or likely to be used, for AI or automated decision support. Turns the GOV.UK AI-ready data guidance into checks at the annual review.
gov: Record the AI task the data supports, whether outputs affect individuals, and which uses are out of scope, such as automated decisions.
Name the owner who approves AI uses, and decide what happens if a use changes.
Publish an algorithmic transparency record where a tool supports decisions about people.
Use the Data and AI Ethics Framework for new or higher-risk uses.

cat.rule: Training, fine-tuning, inference or evaluation: which are allowed
Fields that are personal, confidential or special category
Where the data comes from and how it is produced
Version, so a training set can be reconstructed exactly

rules.rule: Training labels are complete
Label completeness does not differ by more than 5 points between groups
Each record appears once, so training and test sets do not overlap
Numeric features have no implausible outliers

items: The task the data supports is known
It is known whether outputs affect individuals
Out-of-scope uses are stated
A named owner approves AI uses
Permitted uses (training, fine-tuning, inference, evaluation) are known
Sensitive fields are flagged
Permitted working environments are known
There is a plan if the use case changes
Tables and fields are understood
Event time, update frequency and history are clear
Schema changes and versions are tracked
Provenance is known
Known issues and biases are documented
Stable identifiers exist or their absence is stated
Data is machine readable or has an extraction pipeline
Rights, redaction and sensitivity travel with extracted content
Outputs can be traced back to source files
Humans review training data and outputs
Someone owns quality, drift and bias monitoring
Breaks, drift and anomalies are detected
Fixes are re-approved
Training sets can be reconstructed exactly
There is a process if AI causes service, cost or trust issues

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a casework text archive proposed for a summarisation tool. The review finds redaction does not travel with extracted text, so the asset is marked not yet AI-ready and a pipeline fix is added to the DQAP.
risks: Open or available data is not the same as AI-ready data.
Bias in labels or coverage becomes bias in outputs.
Without exact versioning, a model cannot be retrained or audited.
checklist: AI permitted uses and sensitive fields are on the catalogue record
The five areas of the GOV.UK self-assessment are reviewed at the annual review
Group disparity rules are in the DQAP
A transparency record is published where a tool supports decisions about people

supplements.title: Fraud and error
supplements.summary: For assets used to detect fraud or error, where identity matching quality decides who is flagged.
gov: Require a person to review every automated flag before action is taken against someone.
Record the legal power used for each fraud data flow.
Measure and report false positives, not only detections.

cat.term: local extension (one of the seven purposes)
cat.rule: Fraud and error
How records are matched, and the known match error rate

rules.rule: National Insurance number is in a valid format
Each person appears once in the matching base
Date of birth is recorded, so matches are not made on name alone

identifiers.name: National Insurance number
identifiers.format: Two letters, six digits and a letter A to D, with some prefixes not used

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a matching exercise between benefit and payroll data. FRD-03 shows date of birth missing for 4% of records; those records are excluded from automated matching and routed to manual review.
risks: Poor identity data produces false positives that fall on real people.
Names transliterated differently can be missed or mismatched, affecting some communities more than others.
checklist: Human review of flags is required and recorded
False positive rates are measured
Identity field validity rules are in the DQAP

supplements.title: Justice, policing and national security
supplements.summary: For assets in law enforcement, justice, defence or security settings, where only OFFICIAL assets are in scope and metadata itself may be sensitive.
gov: Confirm the classification of the asset and of its metadata; only OFFICIAL assets are in scope of the policy.
Record whether processing falls under Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (law enforcement processing).
Restrict catalogue record visibility where the description itself is sensitive, and record the handling marking.

cat.rule: OFFICIAL, with any handling marking such as OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE
Internal, with the vetting level needed to access the data

rules.rule: Every record carries a classification marking from the allowed list
Event dates are not in the future

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a court listings data asset. The catalogue record is visible across government, but the distribution is restricted, and JUS-01 confirms no records carry a higher marking.
risks: Describing an asset in detail can reveal sensitive capabilities.
Assets above OFFICIAL must not be described in this portal or reported through it.
checklist: Classification of the asset and its metadata is confirmed
Part 3 processing is identified where it applies
Catalogue record visibility matches the sensitivity of the description

supplements.title: Data about people
supplements.summary: For any asset that holds records about individual people. Makes sure forms and rules let people describe themselves accurately.
gov: Collect only the personal fields the purpose needs, and record why each is needed.
Follow current statistical guidance for questions about sex and gender, ethnicity and disability, and offer 'prefer not to say'.
Watch for the cross-government person data and vulnerability data standards and adopt them when published.

cat.rule: Whether the asset holds personal or special category data
Who the records describe, and known gaps in coverage

rules.rule: Family name is recorded
Date of birth is not in the future
Each person is recorded once
Ethnicity is not unknown, where it is lawfully collected

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a customer contact data set. PER-01 fails for records from a form that forced a single name field; the fix is to change the form, not to clean the data.
risks: Forms that cannot record names, addresses or identities accurately create bias at source.
Completeness that looks good overall can hide gaps for some groups.
checklist: Each personal field has a recorded purpose
Forms allow 'prefer not to say' and names in full
Completeness is broken down by group where lawful

supplements.title: Reference data and identifiers
supplements.summary: For assets that depend on code lists and identifiers maintained by other organisations, such as area codes, organisation codes and company numbers.
gov: Name the authoritative source and owner of each code list the asset uses.
Record the version of each code list and how changes are picked up.
Prefer recommended open standards for identifiers.

cat.rule: Each code list and its version

rules.rule: Area code is a GSS code
Company number is in Companies House format
LEI is valid, including its check digits
Charity number is in a valid format

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a grants register. REF-01 fails after a boundary change because the code list was not updated; the fix is to subscribe to the code list's change notices.
risks: Code lists change; stale codes pass format checks but point to retired areas or organisations.
checklist: Every code list has a named source and version
Changes to code lists are picked up on a schedule

supplements.title: Records, retention and disposal
supplements.summary: For every critical data asset that must be kept, archived or destroyed on a schedule. Joins data asset management to records management.
gov: Record the retention schedule and disposal action for each asset in the ownership register.
Agree with the records manager when an asset is retired, archived or transferred.
Keep catalogue records for retired assets, marked as retired, so dependants can see what changed.
When an asset needs to be kept longer than its schedule allows, record the reason and who approved it in the exception register (T-GOV-4), with a review date.

cat.rule: Retention period and disposal action
What replaces a retired asset

rules.rule: Records are not older than the retention period in your schedule (this example uses 7 years)

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a case management extract kept for seven years. REC-01 flags records past retention, which the owner agrees to dispose of through the records management process.
risks: Data kept past its retention period is a data protection risk; data destroyed early is a records risk.

There is no single government-wide retention period. The National Archives describes short, medium and long periods and each organisation sets its own schedule, so check yours before using an example such as seven years.
checklist: Retention and disposal are on the ownership register
Retired assets keep a marked catalogue record
The retention fields in the ownership register (T-GOV-2) and catalogue record (T-CAT-2) are filled in from your organisation's schedule

supplements.title: Data architecture and models
supplements.summary: For critical data assets whose structure others build on. Describes the entities, how they relate and which system is the authoritative source, and links them to the catalogue.
gov: Name the authoritative source for each entity, and the role that approves changes to its structure (the design authority in a change programme).
Keep the entity and relationship list (T-CAT-4) with the asset, and review it when the data model changes.

cat.rule: Link to the published schema or data model
Link to the entity and relationship list or diagram

rules.rule: Each entity's key is unique

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a case management asset with people, cases, appointments and outcomes. The worked entity and relationship list and the diagram drawn from it are with the entity and relationship list template (T-CAT-4); ARC-01 checks each entity key is unique.
risks: Without an agreed authoritative source, two systems can each claim to be the master copy, and returns count assets twice.
Diagrams drawn by hand drift from the real model; keep the list as the source and draw the diagram from it.
checklist: Every entity has a key, a description and an authoritative source
Relationships state their cardinality
The catalogue record links to the list or diagram

supplements.title: Devolved governments and local government
supplements.summary: For assets that flow to or from the devolved governments or councils, which are not bound by the policy but often depend on it.
gov: Record which nations the asset covers and which bodies supply or receive it.
Where a devolved government or council supplies data, agree quality expectations in the sharing agreement, because the policy does not bind them.
Offer councils the playbooks as a voluntary route to adoption.

cat.rule: Nations covered, using GSS codes (England E, Scotland S, Wales W, Northern Ireland N)
Languages of the data and documentation, including Welsh where it applies

rules.rule: Nation is recorded from the allowed list
Area code is a GSS code

four_nations.position: Not bound by the policy; own approach to data sharing governance
Not bound by the policy; own approach to data sharing governance
Not bound by the policy; own approach to data sharing governance

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a UK-wide dataset assembled from four national returns. DEV-01 shows records from one nation coded inconsistently; the fix is agreed with that nation's data team.
risks: Presenting England-only rules as UK-wide misleads users in other nations.
Differences in definitions between nations break comparability.
checklist: Nations covered are on the catalogue record
Quality expectations for devolved or council suppliers are in the agreement

supplements.title: Environmental, sensor and time-series data
supplements.summary: For monitoring and sensor data where readings arrive continuously and gaps, units and drift matter more than missing fields.
gov: Name who owns calibration of instruments as well as who owns the data.
Record how gaps and suspect readings are flagged and whether they are corrected.

cat.rule: The interval between readings
Monitoring sites and their locations

rules.rule: No gaps in the expected reading interval
Every measure column names its unit
Readings have no implausible outliers

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: river level readings every 15 minutes. ENV-01 finds a six-hour gap from a failed sensor; the gap is flagged, not filled, in the published data.
risks: Filling gaps silently makes data look complete when it is not.
Sensor drift passes format checks; it needs calibration records.
checklist: Reading interval and units are on the catalogue record
Gaps and outliers are flagged, not silently corrected

supplements.title: Pupil and learner data
supplements.summary: For assets about pupils and learners, which are long-lived and linked across schools, colleges and nations.
gov: Record the collection the data comes from and its specification version.
Treat records about children with the extra care data protection law expects.

cat.rule: The census or collection specification and version

rules.rule: School unique reference number is 6 digits
Each pupil appears once per census

supplements.example: Illustrative, synthetic: a termly pupil census extract. EDU-02 finds duplicate pupils for dual-registered learners; the rule is refined to count the main registration only.
risks: Dual registration and moves between schools create apparent duplicates.
checklist: The collection specification and version are recorded
Duplicate and dual registration rules are agreed

strands.name: Ownership and governance
levels: Few assets have a named owner; decisions about data are made by whoever holds it.
Owners named for some critical assets, often by job title only; no regular review.
Every reported critical asset has a named owner who knows the role; a board meets and records decisions.
Owners review their assets each year, escalate risks and are covered when people move; ownership is in objectives.
Ownership is routine across the organisation and its bodies; owners shape investment and sharing decisions.

strands.name: Cataloguing and reporting
levels: No list of critical assets; knowledge sits with individuals.
A spreadsheet of assets exists, with gaps in the core metadata.
All in-scope assets are in a catalogue with the core metadata and reported to GDS on time.
Metadata is machine-readable, checked automatically and updated when assets change; arm's length body returns are assured.
The catalogue is the first place people look; metadata flows to central discovery services without rework.

strands.name: Quality management
levels: Quality problems are found by users and fixed one by one.
Some rules exist for some assets; quality is measured occasionally.
Every critical asset has a DQAP covering all 7 steps, with targets and an issue log.
Checks run automatically, root causes are fixed upstream and results are published to users.
Quality is designed in at collection; trends drive investment and prevent new issues.

strands.name: Change and investment
levels: Projects create and retire data without telling anyone responsible for it.
Some programmes ask about data at business case stage, inconsistently.
Business cases, spend control and service assessments ask for DAM evidence; migrations reconcile data.
Assurance plans include DAM checkpoints; benefits are tracked; legacy exits start from the asset register.
Portfolio choices are driven by data asset risk and value, including effects on outcomes for different groups.

plan: List the critical data assets the change will create, change, depend on or retire.
Cost ownership, cataloguing and quality work in the economic and financial cases.
Add data asset risks to the programme risk register.
discover: Check the catalogue for assets that already meet the need before collecting new data.
Agree who will own each new or changed asset.
alpha: Design metadata and quality rules alongside the data model.
Run a data protection impact assessment where personal data is involved.
beta: Catalogue new assets before go-live, with the core metadata.
Write and test the DQAP; reconcile migrated data against the source.
live: Hand ownership, the DQAP and the runbook to named people in business as usual.
Report the asset in the next annual return.
retire: Start from the asset register; decide to migrate, archive or dispose of each asset.

items.title: Put data assets in the business case
items.why: The policy says data must be valued and invested in; business cases are where that money is decided.
actions: Name each critical data asset in scope of the change in the strategic case.
Cost owner, steward and catalogue effort and DQAP remediation in the financial case.
Count avoided duplicate collection and cleansing as benefits in the economic case.
Name the data owner in the management case.
evidence: Asset list in the business case

items.title: Use spend control and service assessments as checkpoints
items.why: Spend control and service assessments already stop work that is not ready; adding DAM evidence costs little.
actions: Add three questions to internal spend control: which assets, who owns them, are they catalogued.
At alpha, show the planned metadata and quality rules; at beta, the catalogue entry and DQAP.

Show the panel that data was considered: who owns each asset, how it is described and quality-planned, the DPIA, and that data professionals and users were involved. You do not need to hand in every template; keep them as your team's working record.
Record the answers so the next return reuses them.

items.title: Write DAM into programme assurance
items.why: Large programmes have integrated assurance plans; DAM checks in them are reviewed with everything else.
actions: Add DAM checkpoints to the integrated assurance and approval plan.
Ask reviewers to check asset ownership, catalogue entries and quality plans at each gate.
Give the senior responsible owner a single line on data asset readiness in highlight reports.

items.title: Plan legacy exits from the asset register
items.why: Legacy systems hold large concentrations of hard-to-reach data; the legacy guidance asks for an asset register first.
actions: Build or update the register of data assets held in the legacy system.
Profile quality before migration and set reconciliation rules for counts, totals and keys.
Decide for each asset: migrate, archive under records rules, or dispose.
Keep the catalogue and ownership in step as each asset moves.

items.title: Target legacy where it blocks outcomes and widens inequalities
items.why: Where poor or locked-in data delays access to services, the people most affected are often those already disadvantaged.
actions: Score each critical asset on legacy risk, quality, reuse value and impact on outcomes.
Check whether gaps or errors fall harder on some groups, using the equality duty.
Fund fixes first where risk, value and inequality overlap.
Report the choice and its reasons to the data governance board.

items.title: Build DAM into contracts
items.why: Suppliers often hold or process critical assets; without contract terms the owner cannot meet the policy.
actions: State who owns the data and its metadata.
Require metadata in an agreed format and quality reporting against the DQAP.
Set data return, format and deletion terms for exit.
Include data protection terms from the procurement policy note.

items.title: Manage data asset risk on the same registers
items.why: The policy relies on risk controls; separate data risk lists are easy to ignore.
actions: Record risks to critical assets on the corporate or programme register.
Link each to the asset, its owner and the senior information risk owner.
Review alongside DQAP results each quarter.

items.title: Hand over to business as usual
items.why: Assets created by projects lose their owner when the project closes unless handover is planned.
actions: Confirm a named business-as-usual owner and steward before the project closes.
Hand over the DQAP, quality rules, runbook and open issues.
Use the ownership model's transition steps and set the next review date.

items.title: Plan people change, not just process change
items.why: New duties fail when people are not told, trained, given time or recognised for them.
actions: Assess who is affected: owners, stewards, custodians, analysts, suppliers.
Put data duties into role descriptions and objectives.
Train each role at the right level and give stewards protected time.
Communicate why the policy matters in terms of services and people, not compliance.

items.title: Show the benefits
items.why: Continued funding depends on evidence that the work changed something.
actions: Agree a few measures before starting, such as reuse requests met, duplicate collections stopped or time spent cleansing.
Take a baseline, then measure each year with the return.
Use proportionate evaluation methods.

items.title: Keep the yearly cycle running in business as usual
items.why: The policy is annual; without a calendar it becomes a scramble before each return.
actions: Set fixed dates for asset review, metadata updates, DQAP review and the board.
Track each owner's actions between returns.
Feed lessons into the next year's priorities.

items.title: Assess maturity and set a target
items.why: A shared maturity measure turns the policy into a plan that can be resourced and tracked.
actions: Run the government data maturity assessment or use the self-assessment here as a first pass.
Set a target level for each DAM strand with dates.
Repeat every one to two years.

items.title: Share and reuse safely across organisations
items.why: Reuse is the point of the policy, but it never removes legal duties or forces sharing.
actions: Check the catalogue for reusable assets before collecting new data.
Use the sharing framework and code for agreements.
Record sharing arrangements against the asset in the catalogue.

items.title: Design out future legacy and lock-in
items.why: Systems bought or built today become tomorrow's legacy unless their data can be moved out without loss or delay.
actions: Require data in open, documented formats with a published schema.
Ask suppliers to show how a full export with metadata works before you sign.
Prefer open standards and APIs that follow the government API standards.
Record each system's exit route against its assets in the catalogue.

items.title: Prepare for a cyber incident affecting a critical asset
items.why: A ransomware attack or breach can corrupt or expose a critical asset; quality plans and owners must be ready.
actions: Mark critical data assets in the incident response plan and asset inventory.
Agree recovery point and recovery time with each data owner.
Test restoring an asset and check its quality afterwards against the DQAP rules.
Agree who tells data users when an asset may be affected.
evidence: Restore test and post-restore quality results

items.title: Use the buying routes and contract terms that protect data
items.why: Most catalogue, quality and platform tools are bought; the route and terms decide who controls the data.
actions: Buy through an established framework where one fits, such as G-Cloud.
Use the model contract schedules for data, security and exit rather than supplier terms.
Make metadata delivery, quality reporting and data return measurable obligations with service credits.
Publish transparency information as the Procurement Act requires.
evidence: Contract data, security and exit schedules

lenses.intro: The DAM Policy is written from a data point of view, but delivering it depends on digital, cyber, technology and commercial teams. Each lens below says what the policy means for that community, what they should ask and do for each capability, and where this portal and the rulebook help.

items.name: Data
items.means: The policy's home lens: identify, describe, own and improve critical data assets, and report them.
questions: Which of our assets are critical, and do we agree why?
Can someone outside our team find, understand and trust each asset from its catalogue entry?
Who decides what good enough means for each asset?

gov: Name an owner and steward for every critical asset.
Run a data governance board that records decisions.
cat: Record the core metadata in a catalogue and report it to GDS.
Use the cross-government Metadata Exchange Model terms.
dq: Write a DQAP for every asset and log issues with priorities.
Publish quality statements users can read.

pitfalls: Treating the return as the goal rather than better-managed data.
items.gap: Covered across the three playbooks, the capability model and the sector supplements.

items.name: Digital and service
items.means: Services create, change and consume critical data. Service teams decide what is collected, how it is validated and what users see.
questions: Which critical assets does our service create or depend on?
Do our forms and validation stop bad data at the point of collection?
Are data services such as APIs documented, catalogued and owned like the data behind them?

gov: Name the data owner as a stakeholder of the service from discovery.
Show DAM evidence at service assessments.
cat: Catalogue data services and APIs alongside the data sets they expose.
Publish API documentation that follows the government API standards.
dq: Turn quality rules into form validation and API contract tests.
Design forms so people can describe themselves accurately.

pitfalls: Collecting data the catalogue shows another service already holds.
Treating an API as technical plumbing with no owner.
items.gap: Strengthened in 1.6 with data service and API actions; user research with service teams is still to do (OR-04).

items.name: Cyber and security
items.means: Critical data assets are among the things most worth protecting. Security teams need to know which they are, and data teams need to know an asset can be recovered and trusted after an incident.
questions: Do our asset inventory and incident plans include every critical data asset?
What is the recovery point and recovery time for each one, and who agreed it?
After a restore, how do we know the data is complete and correct?

gov: Link each critical asset to its CAF outcomes and to the SIRO's risk register.
Agree recovery objectives with each data owner.
cat: Record classification, handling caveats and access rights accurately; scope depends on them.
Keep the catalogue itself access-controlled where entries reveal sensitive holdings.
dq: After any restore or suspected tampering, rerun the DQAP rules before the asset is used again.
Treat unexplained quality drops as a possible security signal.

pitfalls: Assuming OFFICIAL means low risk; aggregation can raise sensitivity.
A catalogue that becomes a map for attackers.
items.gap: Was the thinnest lens. 1.6 adds a cyber resilience capability, an incident practice and seven verified security sources. Needs review by a security professional.

items.name: Technology and architecture
items.means: Platforms, integration and tooling decide whether critical data can be found, joined, checked and moved. Architecture choices made now set the cost of the next migration.
questions: Which systems and platforms hold each critical asset?
Can metadata be harvested automatically rather than typed in?
Are quality checks automated in the pipeline, or done by hand?

gov: Record the system of record and data platform for each asset.
Apply the Technology Code of Practice and Cloud First when assets move.
cat: Harvest metadata from platforms into the catalogue using DCAT and the Metadata Exchange Model.
Expose catalogue entries through an API so central discovery services can collect them.
dq: Run quality rules automatically in data pipelines and publish results.
Version schemas and test changes against the DQAP rules before release.

pitfalls: Buying a catalogue tool before agreeing ownership and metadata.
Bespoke integrations that only one supplier understands.
items.gap: Strengthened in 1.6 with architecture, platform and automation actions and verified sources.

items.name: Commercial and suppliers
items.means: Many critical assets are held or processed by suppliers, and most tools are bought. Contracts decide who owns the data, what metadata and quality evidence the supplier must provide, and whether the data can leave.
questions: Which critical assets are held or processed by a supplier?
Does each contract name the data owner and require metadata, quality reporting and full data return?
When does each contract end, and is the exit plan tested?

gov: Map contracts to the critical assets they touch, with end dates.
Use model contract schedules for data, security and exit.
cat: Make catalogue-ready metadata a contract deliverable, in the government's terms.
Require suppliers to keep catalogue entries current when they change the data.
dq: Turn DQAP targets into service levels with credits.
Require suppliers to report quality against the agreed rules.

pitfalls: Supplier terms that treat government data as the supplier's product.
Exit plans that are never tested until the contract ends.
items.gap: Was thin, with one practice. 1.6 adds a buying-routes practice and verified commercial sources. Needs review by a commercial professional.

items.name: Legacy and technical debt
items.means: Legacy systems concentrate critical data that is hard to find, understand or trust, and that blocks better services. Getting data out safely, and not creating the next legacy, are both DAM work.
questions: Where are our largest concentrations of critical data in legacy systems?
Which of them block outcomes for the people who most need services?
What will stop the replacement becoming legacy in its turn?

gov: Prioritise exits where legacy risk, value and inequality overlap.
Keep ownership in step as assets migrate.
cat: Start every exit from the data asset register, as the legacy guidance asks.
Record schemas and lineage before the old system goes.
dq: Profile quality before migration and reconcile counts, totals and keys after.
Use migration as the moment to fix root causes, not copy them.

pitfalls: Migrating data without its meaning or quality history.
Replacing one closed system with another.
items.gap: Covered by the delivery and change practices; 1.6 adds future-legacy prevention.

dama.intro: The Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK) arranges data management as knowledge areas around data governance. This view places the DAM Policy, the capability model and the government maturity model on that wheel, so each role can see which areas it shapes and how the policy fits a wider enterprise data management capability.

areas.desc: Decision rights, accountability and policy for data across the organisation.
areas.im: Information governance and the information asset owner role.

uses.coo: Run the governance cycle and the return
uses.own: Make and record decisions for your assets
uses.stw: Prepare decisions and keep definitions agreed
uses.cat: Apply governance decisions in the catalogue
uses.prg: Bring programme decisions into the governance cycle

uses.coo: Use it to find candidate assets

uses.dql: Trace quality problems to where data enters

uses.cdo: Expect agreed definitions for critical assets
uses.own: Approve the meaning of key data items

uses.cdo: Fund resilient platforms for critical data
uses.coo: Know which platform holds each asset
uses.cat: Record system of record and location

areas.im: Protective marking and access to records.

uses.cdo: Link critical assets to cyber risk
uses.coo: Confirm classification is right before reporting
uses.own: Accept residual risk for your assets
uses.dql: Treat odd quality drops as security signals
uses.prg: Build security in from the start

uses.cdo: Back open standards and shared identifiers

areas.name: Document and content management
areas.desc: Managing unstructured information: documents, content and records.
areas.im: The core of records management: capture, classification, retention and disposal.

uses.coo: Reconcile the asset register with the information asset register
uses.cat: Record retention and disposal in entries
uses.dql: Check documents behind key data items
uses.prg: Plan records transfer when systems retire

areas.desc: Agreeing and maintaining the shared, authoritative versions of key entities and code lists.

uses.dql: Check codes against the reference list

areas.im: Retention of reports and derived records.

uses.own: Know where your data is reused
uses.cat: Catalogue analytical products that are critical

areas.desc: Describing data so people and machines can find, understand and trust it.
areas.im: Records metadata (ISO 23081) and the information asset register.

uses.cdo: Require complete metadata for the return
uses.coo: Build the return from catalogue records
uses.cat: Run the catalogue and harvest metadata

areas.name: Data quality
areas.desc: Defining, measuring and improving how fit data is for its purposes.

uses.cdo: Fund fixes where quality blocks outcomes

Validate at collection; catalogue on creation

A full drill-down would take every reader from a knowledge area to its activities, and from an activity to its tasks, roles, templates, measures and standards, as the three DAM playbooks already do. This is an assessment by this portal, not a commitment.

joinup.intro: Data asset management needs data, records and information, security, digital, technology, analysis, commercial and delivery professionals to act on the same assets. These recommendations turn that into shared artefacts, routines and networks, each with a tangible outcome you can check.

recs.title: Keep one register of assets
recs.action: Reconcile the critical data asset list with the information asset register so each asset has one record, with the data owner and information asset owner linked.
recs.outcome: One list used by data, records and security teams; no asset is reported twice or missed.
recs.measure: Assets on both lists without a shared identifier: zero.

recs.title: Use one glossary
recs.action: Publish one organisation glossary for data, records and security terms, linked to the cross-government vocabulary, and point catalogue entries to it.
recs.outcome: The same word means the same thing in a catalogue entry, a file plan and a risk register.
recs.measure: Critical assets whose key items link to glossary terms.

recs.title: Run one board for data, information and security risk
recs.action: Bring the data governance board, information assurance and the senior information risk owner together, quarterly, with one agenda covering critical assets.
recs.outcome: Decisions on an asset consider data, records and security together.
recs.measure: Decisions recorded per quarter that cite more than one discipline.

recs.title: Put DAM checkpoints in every programme
recs.action: Agree with the programme office a standard set of DAM checks for business cases, gates and handover, and give programmes a named data contact.
recs.outcome: Programmes stop creating unowned, uncatalogued assets.
recs.measure: Programmes closing with every in-scope asset owned, catalogued and quality-planned.

recs.title: Align retention with the data life cycle
recs.action: Map retention schedules to critical assets and record retention and disposal in catalogue entries.
recs.outcome: Data is kept as long as needed and no longer, with evidence.
recs.measure: Critical assets with a recorded retention rule.

recs.title: Learn together
recs.action: Run a shared induction for owners, stewards, information asset owners and programme leads, using the recommended curriculum and this portal's modules.
recs.outcome: People in different professions use the same method and language.
recs.measure: Owners and stewards who completed the shared induction.

recs.title: Join the right communities
recs.action: Give each role one community to join and one to watch, from the list on this page, and share what you learn at the board.
recs.outcome: Practice spreads across organisations instead of being reinvented.
recs.measure: Roles with a named community; lessons shared per quarter.

recs.title: Rehearse an incident together
recs.action: Run a joint exercise where a critical asset is corrupted or exposed, involving security, records, data quality and the owner.
recs.outcome: Everyone knows their part in recovering and re-trusting an asset.
recs.measure: Critical assets covered by a tested recovery and quality check.

recs.title: Share contract clauses
recs.action: Keep a shared library of data, metadata, quality and exit clauses with the commercial team and reuse it in every relevant procurement.
recs.outcome: Suppliers face the same data obligations everywhere.
recs.measure: New contracts touching critical assets that use the shared clauses.

recs.title: Report one set of measures
recs.action: Combine catalogue completeness, DQAP status, records compliance and security assurance for critical assets into one quarterly view.
recs.outcome: Leaders see one picture of how well critical assets are managed.
recs.measure: Quarterly view produced and discussed at the board.

reuse.intro: The portal is built to be reused. Pick the approach that fits how your organisation shares knowledge, from a simple link on your intranet to your own branded copy, an AI assistant or an integration through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Content is published under the Open Government Licence and code under the MIT licence.

approaches.title: Link from your intranet
approaches.what: Stable addresses for every page, tab, step and capability.
how: Link to a page, or to a section with its anchor, for example governance.html#method.
Share links with the Share button on any page.
Point staff to the role routes and the testing page.
approaches.when: You want staff to use the guidance as it is, always current.
cautions: Links go to a prototype that is not official guidance; say so on your intranet.

approaches.title: Embed pages in your intranet or Teams
approaches.what: Show portal pages inside SharePoint, an intranet page or a Microsoft Teams tab.
how: Add a web part or a Teams website tab pointing at a page address.
Choose pages that work well on their own, such as a playbook or the self-assessment.
Keep the prototype banner visible.
approaches.when: You want the content inside the tools people already use.
cautions: Progress and display choices are kept per browser, so they do not follow people between devices.

approaches.title: Read-only data API
approaches.what: Every dataset is a stable file you can fetch from code: JSON, CSV, Turtle and YAML, with cross-site access allowed.
how: Start from the catalogue at data/catalogue.jsonld.
Fetch data/playbooks.json for the full content, or a single CSV.
Pin to a release by recording the version in the catalogue.
approaches.when: You want to build your own views, dashboards or tools on the content.
cautions: Files change with each release; check the version and the What is new page before relying on a field.

approaches.title: Harvest into a data catalogue
approaches.what: A DCAT 3 catalogue other catalogues can harvest, such as CKAN or your own metadata platform.
how: Point your harvester at data/catalogue.jsonld or data/catalogue.ttl.
Map dataset identifiers to your own scheme.
approaches.when: You run a catalogue and want the playbook datasets listed alongside your own.
cautions: Treat harvested entries as reference material, not as your own critical assets.

approaches.title: Load into enterprise content and collaboration tools
approaches.what: Bring templates, checklists and actions into SharePoint lists, Confluence, Planner or your tracker.
how: Import a CSV, such as change-checklist.csv or templates.csv, into a list or board.
Link each item back to its page for the full guidance.
Agree an owner to refresh it after each release.
approaches.when: You want teams to work from tasks and templates in their own tools.
cautions: Copies go out of date; note the version you imported.

approaches.title: White-label your own copy
approaches.what: Run your own branded copy with your organisation's name, colours, tone and extra content.
how: Fork the repository on GitHub.
Change the title, contact form and site address in the content file, and colours in the style sheet.
Edit or add content in the content files; the build checks every reference.
Publish with the included workflow on your own GitHub Pages or web server.
approaches.when: You need the guidance in your own house style, or with local procedures added.
cautions: Keep the attribution statement and the licences.
Your copy no longer gets updates automatically; merge new releases deliberately.

approaches.title: Adapt for your audiences and language
approaches.what: Tailor wording, examples and depth for particular audiences, or translate, for example into Welsh.
how: Copy the content files and adjust text, keeping identifiers so links still work.
Use the plain English and style checks in the build to keep quality up.
approaches.when: Your audiences need different language, tone or examples.
cautions: Translations need a named owner to keep them in step with releases.

approaches.title: Ask an AI assistant about the portal
approaches.what: Use an AI assistant or chatbot to answer questions from the portal, alongside the built-in search.
how: Give the assistant the address of llms.txt, a short guide written for AI tools, or llms-full.txt with the full text.
Or add the portal website, or data/playbooks.json, as a knowledge source in a tool such as Microsoft Copilot Studio.
Ask it to cite the page each answer comes from.
approaches.when: You want people to ask questions in their own words.
cautions: AI answers can be wrong; check them against the page cited, and against GOV.UK, which is the authority.
Do not paste personal or sensitive data into public AI tools.

approaches.title: Connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
approaches.what: A small reference MCP server in the repository lets AI assistants search the portal and fetch capabilities, requirements, practices and sector rules as structured data, with links to their pages.
how: Run integrations/mcp/server.py with Python 3; it needs no extra packages.
Add it as an MCP server in an MCP-compatible assistant.
Point it at the live site or at a local copy of data/playbooks.json.
approaches.when: You want an assistant or agent to use the portal's content as a tool, with sources.
cautions: It is a reference implementation for testing, not a supported service.
Host it inside your own environment if you add internal content.

approaches.title: Connectors, add-ons and plugins
approaches.what: Use the open data and the MCP server as the basis for a connector, add-on or plugin in your organisation's platforms.
how: Use the catalogue and JSON files as the data source.
Wrap the MCP server or the files in your platform's connector or plugin format.
Register it through your organisation's approval process for integrations.
approaches.when: You want the content inside a business application or an AI assistant your organisation already uses.
cautions: Follow your organisation's rules for approving third-party integrations.

tooling.intro: Most organisations run several tools for data asset management, often from different suppliers, and many are offered a bundled suite. This page sets out the kinds of tool involved, the open standards and patterns that let them work together, where bundles and contracts create lock-in, and questions to ask in a request for information (RFI) or tender, framed by what the DAM Policy needs. It names no products and endorses none; for named products and a fuller question builder, see the related links at the end of this page.
principles: Your metadata, glossary, quality rules, lineage and results are your data. Make sure you can get all of them out, in open formats, at any time and at no extra charge.
Prefer open standards at the boundaries between tools, even when the tools come from one supplier. That keeps the option to replace one part without replacing the rest.
Buy capabilities, not bundles. Price, evaluate and be able to exit each capability separately.
Prove interoperability before you sign. A round-trip test with your own data is worth more than a list of connectors.
Plan the exit at the start: cost it, time it and write it into the contract and business case.

categories.name: Data catalogue and metadata management
categories.what: Records what data assets exist, what they mean, who owns them and how they can be used; harvests technical metadata from data platforms.
categories.ask: Can every catalogue record, including custom fields, owners and classifications, be exported as DCAT and imported into another catalogue without loss?

categories.name: Business glossary and vocabularies
categories.what: Holds agreed business terms, definitions, synonyms and hierarchies, and links them to data assets.
categories.ask: Can the glossary be exported and imported as SKOS, keeping broader and narrower terms and links to assets?

categories.name: Data quality profiling, rules and monitoring
categories.what: Profiles data, runs quality rules, scores dimensions, raises issues and tracks remediation.
categories.ask: Are rules held in a readable, exportable form, and can results be published as DQV or through an open API for a catalogue to show?

categories.name: Lineage and data observability
categories.what: Shows where data comes from, how it moves and changes, and whether pipelines ran as expected.
categories.ask: Does the tool emit and accept OpenLineage events, including from pipelines and platforms the supplier does not own?

categories.name: Reference and master data management
categories.what: Holds the golden record for entities such as organisations, people, places and products, and the reference lists that other systems share.
categories.ask: Can master and reference data, with match and survivorship rules and history, be extracted in an open format and served through a documented API?

categories.name: Governance workflow, policy and access
categories.what: Manages stewardship tasks, approvals, data sharing requests, classification and access policies.
categories.ask: Can classifications and access policies be read by other tools through an API, and does the tool use your identity provider rather than its own user store?

categories.name: Data contracts and data products
categories.what: Describes what a data producer promises consumers, such as schema, quality thresholds, owners and service levels.
categories.ask: Are contracts stored as ODCS files you can keep in your own repository, and can more than one tool enforce them?

categories.name: Records and content management
categories.what: Manages documents and records, retention and disposal, and transfer to an archive.
categories.ask: Can retention and disposal decisions and record metadata be shared with the data catalogue, so a data asset and its records follow one schedule?

categories.name: AI assistants and search over metadata
categories.what: Lets people ask questions of the catalogue, glossary and quality results in plain language.
categories.ask: Can an assistant your organisation already approves read the catalogue through an open protocol or documented API, respecting the same access rules?

patterns.name: Scan and harvest
patterns.how: The catalogue or lineage tool connects to a database, warehouse, file store or business intelligence tool and reads its technical metadata on a schedule.
patterns.when: Building and refreshing the inventory of technical assets.
patterns.watch: Connectors are often licensed separately, priced per source, or maintained only for the supplier's own platform. Ask who maintains each one and how quickly it follows new versions.

patterns.name: Documented API
patterns.how: One tool reads or writes another's records through a published API, described in OpenAPI, with the same access controls as the user interface.
patterns.when: Showing quality scores in the catalogue, creating issues, syncing owners or terms.
patterns.watch: Check rate limits, whether every object is available through the API (not only some), and whether API calls are charged.

patterns.name: Events and webhooks
patterns.how: A tool publishes an event when something changes, such as a rule failing, a pipeline running or an asset being classified, and others subscribe.
patterns.when: Near real-time alerts, lineage capture and keeping several tools in step.
patterns.watch: Prefer open event formats such as OpenLineage over supplier-specific payloads.

patterns.name: Open file exchange
patterns.how: Export and import in open formats such as DCAT (JSON-LD or Turtle), SKOS, CSV with CSVW, or ODCS YAML.
patterns.when: Migration, exit, bulk loading, publishing and sharing with other organisations.
patterns.watch: Exports that drop custom fields, history or links are a form of lock-in. Test a full round trip.

patterns.name: Contract-driven checks
patterns.how: Producers publish a data contract; quality and pipeline tools read the same file to check data, and the catalogue shows it.
patterns.when: Agreeing what consumers can rely on, and checking it automatically.
patterns.watch: Contract formats are still maturing; keep contracts in your own repository, not only inside a tool.

patterns.name: Embedded views
patterns.how: One tool shows another's information in place, for example quality results on a catalogue page.
patterns.when: Giving users one place to look without copying data.
patterns.watch: Embedding through a supplier's private integration can hide a dependency that breaks when either tool changes.

patterns.name: Shared identity and access
patterns.how: All tools sign users in through your identity provider and take roles and groups from it.
patterns.when: Always. It keeps ownership and stewardship roles consistent across tools.
patterns.watch: Some products charge more for single sign-on or automated user provisioning; ask early.

patterns.name: AI access through an open protocol
patterns.how: An assistant reads the catalogue, glossary and quality results through a documented API or a Model Context Protocol server.
patterns.when: Plain-language questions over metadata, with answers that cite their source.
patterns.watch: Make sure the assistant respects access rules and that prompts and answers stay in your approved environment.

pairs.flows: Quality scores, rule results and open issues shown against each asset; asset owners and definitions used by quality rules.
pairs.open: DQV for results, ODCS for rules and thresholds, documented APIs.
pairs.fallback: Scheduled export of results as CSV, matched on a shared asset identifier.
pairs.watch: Without a shared, persistent asset identifier the two tools drift apart.

pairs.flows: Where data comes from, where it goes and which jobs change it.
pairs.fallback: Harvest lineage from the platform's own logs.
pairs.watch: Lineage limited to one supplier's platform hides the rest of the journey.

pairs.flows: Business terms linked to assets and columns.
pairs.open: SKOS for the vocabulary; DCAT themes and keywords for links.
pairs.fallback: CSV term lists with stable identifiers.
pairs.watch: Terms stored as free text cannot be reused elsewhere.

pairs.flows: Which assets hold the golden record and which are copies; reference lists used in metadata.
pairs.open: Documented APIs; SKOS for reference lists.
pairs.fallback: Record the authoritative source as catalogue metadata.
pairs.watch: Bundled master data and catalogue modules often share a private model that is hard to separate.

pairs.flows: Retention, disposal and record metadata for data assets that are also records.
pairs.fallback: A shared retention schedule identifier recorded in both tools.
pairs.watch: Two retention schedules for the same information leads to unlawful keeping or early disposal.

pairs.flows: Rules run as data moves; failed checks stop or flag a load.
pairs.fallback: Rules called from the pipeline through a documented API.
pairs.watch: Rules written in a proprietary language cannot move with you.

pairs.between: Governance workflow and identity and access
pairs.flows: Owners, stewards, approvals and access decisions.
pairs.open: Your identity provider's standard protocols; documented APIs.
pairs.fallback: Scheduled sync of roles from the human resources or identity system.
pairs.watch: Local user stores create orphaned owners when people leave.

pairs.flows: Published and shared dataset descriptions, harvested by national catalogues.
pairs.open: DCAT, schema.org Dataset and the Metadata Exchange Model.
pairs.fallback: Publish a CSV catalogue with documented columns.
pairs.watch: Private catalogue formats block harvesting by data.gov.uk and the National Data Library.

pairs.flows: Questions answered from catalogue, glossary and quality information, with links back.
pairs.fallback: Publish a text export for an approved assistant to index.
pairs.watch: An assistant that bypasses catalogue access rules can disclose restricted metadata.

pros: One contract, one support route and one user interface.
Integrations between modules usually work on day one.
Can be quicker to start for a small team.
cons: Modules share a private metadata model, so replacing one part means replacing all of it.
Weaker modules are carried by stronger ones, and evaluated less carefully.
Pricing across modules is hard to compare with separate tools.
Connectors to other suppliers' tools are fewer, slower or charged extra.
The exit cost grows with every module adopted.
tests: Could you replace the data quality module next year and keep the catalogue? What would it cost?
Are the module prices shown separately, and can you drop a module at renewal without penalty?
Do the modules use the same open standards between themselves that they offer to other tools?

barriers.name: Pricing metric that punishes growth
barriers.detail: Charges per asset, per scanned table, per rule run or per user can make cataloguing everything, or running quality checks often, unaffordable. The DAM Policy expects broad coverage.
barriers.mitigate: Model cost at three and five times today's volume; prefer prices tied to things you control; cap annual increases.

barriers.name: Shared credits or consumption pools
barriers.detail: Credits spread across modules make it hard to see what each capability costs and easy to overspend.
barriers.mitigate: Ask for a price per capability and a monthly usage report you can export.

barriers.name: Connectors and APIs charged extra
barriers.detail: Some connectors, API access, single sign-on or automated user provisioning sit in higher tiers.
barriers.mitigate: List every integration you need in the requirement and require them in the evaluated price.

barriers.name: Export and exit charges
barriers.detail: Fees or effort to get data and metadata out, including cloud egress charges, make exit costly. The CMA found egress fees and interoperability barriers restrict switching in public cloud.
barriers.mitigate: Require complete export in open formats at any time at no extra charge, and an exit plan with supplier support in the contract.

barriers.name: Ownership of rules, terms and lineage
barriers.detail: Contracts can leave quality rules, glossary content, classifications or derived lineage as the supplier's property or in a form only their tool can read.
barriers.mitigate: State that all content you or the tool create about your data is yours, and must be exportable.

barriers.name: Platform and marketplace commitments
barriers.detail: Buying through a cloud marketplace against a spend commitment can tie a catalogue or quality tool to one cloud platform.
barriers.mitigate: Check the tool runs and is supported on other platforms, and that the commitment does not lengthen the term.

barriers.name: Licence terms that limit where software runs
barriers.detail: Licensing that costs more on a rival cloud reduces choice. The CMA has raised concerns about business software licensing in cloud.
barriers.mitigate: Ask for licence terms that are the same wherever the software runs.

barriers.name: Long terms, auto-renewal and price uplift
barriers.detail: Multi-year terms, automatic renewal and uncapped increases reduce your bargaining power at exactly the point you might switch.
barriers.mitigate: Use break points, notice periods you can meet, and capped increases; diarise renewal decisions a year ahead.

items: Which open standards does the product read and write for catalogue records, glossaries, quality results, lineage and data contracts? Give versions.
Can we export everything, including custom fields, history, owners, classifications, comments and links, at any time, in open formats, without supplier help or extra charge?
Describe a round trip, exporting our catalogue as DCAT and re-importing it into another product. What is lost?
Does the product support the government Metadata Exchange Model for critical data assets?
Is every object and action in the user interface available through a documented API? Provide the OpenAPI description.
List each connector, who builds and maintains it, its licence and price, and how quickly it follows new versions of the connected system.
Which connectors exist for other suppliers' catalogues, quality tools, lineage tools and records systems?
Does the product emit and accept OpenLineage events? Can it read ODCS data contracts?
What rate limits, call charges or tier limits apply to APIs and events?
Confirm that metadata, glossary terms, quality rules, scores, lineage and any content the product derives from our data belong to us.
In what form are quality rules held? Can they be read and run outside the product?
Can we keep data contracts and rules in our own code repository and have the product read them from there?
Give separate prices for each capability, and confirm we can stop any one at renewal without penalty.
Model the price at today's volumes and at three and five times them.
Which features, connectors, single sign-on or provisioning sit in higher tiers?
What does exit involve, how long does it take, what support is included, and what does it cost, including any cloud egress?
Are licence prices the same on any cloud or on our own infrastructure?
Does the product use our identity provider for sign-in and automated user provisioning, at no extra charge?
Can classification and access policies be read by other tools?
If the product includes AI features, where are prompts and answers processed and stored, are they used to train models, and can they be switched off?
Can an assistant we already approve query the product through an open protocol, respecting the same access rules?
Name customers who use the product with another supplier's catalogue, quality or lineage tool, and how they connect them.
Will you take part in a short proof of concept using our data and an interoperability test we define?

steps.name: Map what you have
steps.text: List the tools in use or planned for each capability, who owns them, contract end dates and how they connect today.

steps.name: Set the boundaries
steps.text: Decide which open standard sits at each boundary between capabilities, using the pairs on this page, and record it as an architecture decision.

steps.name: Run an RFI
steps.text: Use the questions on this page. Search Find a Tender and G-Cloud for how other bodies specified similar tools.

backlog.story: As a data owner, I need retention and disposal recorded with each asset, so that data is neither kept too long nor destroyed early.

mvp.condition: Keep the fields optional and out of the return template; agree read-across to records schedules with the government knowledge and information management team.

backlog.story: As a data owner, I need a data sharing agreement that covers the lawful basis and legal gateway, so that shared critical assets are on a sound footing.

backlog.story: As a data architect, I need to describe a critical asset's entities, relationships and authoritative source, so that others can build on it and returns do not count it twice.

mvp.condition: Only the authoritative source question belongs in the MVP, because it helps apply the policy's source data test; the rest follows the baseline return.

mvp.condition: Signposts now; complete with the pilot's feedback and an expert review (BL-14) before implementation begins in January 2027.

mvp.usability: Governance, metadata and data quality already drill down to their playbook steps; the other areas would add reading that most organisations do not need for the return.
mvp.condition: Build the structure with data architecture first (BL-36). Add other areas only when the profession that owns each agrees to own its content.

backlog.story: As a data architect or design authority, I need a step-by-step playbook for data architecture, so that critical assets have a known structure and authoritative source that others can build on.

mvp.usability: Useful to architects; owners and coordinators need only the authoritative source question, which is already in the cataloguing guidance and the supplement.
mvp.condition: Phase 2, from January 2027, once architecture leads agree to own and review it; see the assessment on the DAMA wheel.

bodies.intro: Who decides, who advises and where practitioners meet, for data asset management in UK government. Each entry says what the body is for, how it relates to the DAM Policy and how you can take part. Facts were checked on GOV.UK and data.gov.uk on 5 November 2026; where terms of reference are not published, it says so.

flow.does: Spot problems, share practice and help develop proposals

items.name: Chief Data Officer (CDO) Council
items.purpose: The decision-making body overseeing strategic delivery of Mission 3 of the National Data Strategy (government's own use of data).
aims: Collective accountability for government's own use and reuse of data
Set future strategy as targets are met
Help the Data Standards Authority identify strategic risks, problems and opportunities for common standards
items.outcomes: Strategic direction for data across government; it does not set specific data standards.
items.dam: DAM Policy artefacts such as the Data Ownership Model are presented to the CDO Council and its Executive before adoption.
items.engage: Through your organisation's chief data officer or equivalent senior data leader. Raise issues with them; the council is not open to direct membership.
items.tor: Terms of reference not found published on GOV.UK.

items.name: Data Standards Authority (DSA) Steering Board
items.purpose: A senior advisory group that supports the Data Standards Authority in setting cross-government data standardisation strategy and delivery plans.
aims: Oversee the DSA's operations and priorities
Approve cross-government standards as the final step of endorsement
items.outcomes: Endorsed data standards for central government, and their implementation in member organisations.
items.dam: Endorsed the data quality action plan guidance and was presented the essential shared data assets policy and Data Ownership Model, which the DAM Policy builds on.

items.engage: Through your organisation's representative, or by bringing evidence to a community that feeds it.
items.tor: Role set out in the DSA operational model; minutes published.

involve.intro: This portal is built in the open, and anyone can help: use it and tell us what works, test it, suggest and vote for ideas, improve the content, review it as an expert, or champion it in your own team. Every way of taking part is recognised with a badge.
rules: Follow the code of conduct. Be kind, assume good faith and stay on topic.
Nothing above OFFICIAL, no personal data, and no email addresses anywhere.
Name roles, not people. Credit is given by GitHub username, only if you choose.
Every fact needs a source and a provenance label (see How sources are labelled).
Anyone can suggest a change. The owner reviews every change before it is published, and nobody is added as a collaborator except by the owner's invitation.
Decisions are made in the open, through the roadmap and the decisions log on Have your say.

The DAM capability playbooks are a prototype website that helps organisations meet the Data Asset Management Policy. It sets out the steps for each role in data governance, data cataloguing and data quality, with templates, a capability model and links to GOV.UK guidance.

The team is looking for people to test it, take part in research, and suggest ideas. Find out more: {site}research.html

It is not official GOV.UK guidance. Where it repeats GOV.UK, the GOV.UK page is the authority.
